# Ormoc City CDRRMO–EOC Manual of Operations

> **Consolidated Draft 1.0 (12 November 2026), revised for consistency on 25 November 2026.** Controlled working draft for technical, institutional and legal validation. No part is approved City policy until adopted through the proper instrument. Consolidates the Executive Summary, the Introduction and Chapters 1 to 10, with Annex A.

**VISUAL EVIDENCE STANDARD** Charts reproduce only values stated in the controlled draft or workbook references. Conceptual diagrams are explanatory models, not measured results. Unvalidated scores, proposed workflows and legal readings remain explicitly provisional.

# Glossary of Terms

The definitions below explain how key terms are used in this Manual. They are provided for operational consistency and ease of reference. Where a term has a definition or rule in a statute, regulation or official issuance, that authoritative text prevails. This glossary does not create, enlarge or transfer any legal power.

| **Term**                                                               | **Meaning as Used in This Manual**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **After-action review (AAR)**                                          | A structured review conducted after an incident, operation, exercise or activity to identify what worked, what did not, why it happened, and what corrective actions are required.                                                                                                                     |
| **Alert level**                                                        | The operational status used to communicate the readiness posture of the response system. In this Manual, White means normal operations; Blue means at least 50% of resources are on standby (partial EOC activation); and Red means all resources are available (full EOC activation).                 |
| **Anticipatory action (AA)**                                           | Actions taken ahead of an anticipated hazard impact, based on an agreed trigger or forecast, to reduce expected humanitarian impacts. The applicable legal authority, trigger, lead time and funding rules must be verified against current national issuances.                                        |
| **Barangay Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committee (BDRRMC)** | The barangay-level committee responsible for coordinating disaster risk reduction and management within its jurisdiction, consistent with the roles and arrangements set out in the Manual.                                                                                                            |
| **Build Back Better (BBB)**                                            | An approach to recovery, rehabilitation and reconstruction that uses the recovery process to reduce future disaster risk and strengthen resilience, rather than simply restoring pre-disaster conditions.                                                                                              |
| **Camp coordination and camp management (CCCM)**                       | The coordination and management arrangements for evacuation centres and displacement sites, including site-level coordination, service access, protection, information and management responsibilities.                                                                                                |
| **Corrective and preventive action (CAPA)**                            | A documented improvement action intended to address the cause of an identified nonconformity or gap and prevent recurrence. Closure requires evidence that the action was completed and effective.                                                                                                     |
| **Climate and disaster risk assessment (CDRA)**                        | An assessment that brings together climate and disaster hazards, exposure, vulnerability and capacity information to inform land-use, development, investment and DRRM decisions.                                                                                                                      |
| **City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (CDRRMC)**       | The City's statutory DRRM policy, coordination and oversight body. The Manual distinguishes the Council's governance and recommendation functions from the CDRRMO's permanent technical and operational functions.                                                                                     |
| **City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO)**        | The City's permanent technical and operational office for disaster risk reduction and management and the secretariat of the CDRRMC. It supports planning, coordination, preparedness, response and other functions assigned by law and valid City issuances.                                           |
| **Disaster**                                                           | A serious disruption of the functioning of a community or society arising from hazardous events interacting with exposure, vulnerability and capacity, resulting in human, material, economic or environmental losses and impacts.                                                                     |
| **Disaster risk**                                                      | The potential for disaster-related losses, determined by the interaction of hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity. Risk is context-specific and changes as these factors change.                                                                                                                |
| **Disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM)**                      | The systematic process of identifying, assessing and reducing disaster risks, preparing for and responding to emergencies, and supporting recovery, rehabilitation and resilience-building.                                                                                                            |
| **Emergency Operations Center (EOC)**                                  | An activated coordination mechanism through which authorised officials and participating offices coordinate information, priorities, resources and operational support during an emergency. In this Manual, the EOC is not a field command post and is not a fourth CDRRMO division.                   |
| **Exposure**                                                           | The presence of people, infrastructure, housing, livelihoods, services and other assets in places that could be adversely affected by a hazard.                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Hazard**                                                             | A process, phenomenon or human activity that may cause loss of life, injury or other health impacts, property damage, social and economic disruption, or environmental degradation.                                                                                                                    |
| **Incident Command System (ICS)**                                      | A standardised on-scene incident management approach that provides an organisational structure, roles and processes for managing incident operations. The ICS/Incident Management Team manages field operations; the EOC supports coordination and resource decisions without replacing field command. |
| **Incident Command Post (ICP)**                                        | The location from which the Incident Commander and incident management organisation direct on-scene operations. The Manual maintains a functional distinction between the ICP and the EOC.                                                                                                             |
| **Institutional Assessment Tool (IAT)**                                | The assessment instrument used in the Manual's institutional baseline and improvement cycle. The controlled IAT v1.7 workbook contains 140 indicators across 22 domains, organised into CDRRMO, EOC and interface components.                                                                          |
| **Institutional Maturity Index (IMI)**                                 | A weighted index calculated from scored IAT indicators to summarise institutional maturity. The Manual reports the CDRRMO and EOC components together for the overall IMI and reports the Part C interface index separately.                                                                           |
| **Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund (LDRRMF)**         | The local fund established under the Philippine DRRM framework to support disaster risk reduction and management activities, subject to applicable budgeting, accounting, procurement and audit rules.                                                                                                 |
| **Manual of Operations (MOO)**                                         | This controlled document setting out the governance arrangements, roles, procedures, decision rules, records and performance expectations for the Ormoc City CDRRMO and EOC.                                                                                                                           |
| **Master Procedure Register**                                          | The Manual's consolidated index of standard operating procedures and workflows, showing their chapter, process owner, quality stage and key record.                                                                                                                                                    |
| **MODE**                                                               | The Manual of Operations for the DRRMO and EOC platform referred to in the Manual. It is the digital platform intended to support controlled procedures, records, workflows and monitoring; platform configuration does not itself confer legal authority.                                             |
| **OpCen**                                                              | The CDRRMO Operations Center. The Manual describes the EOC as an activated coordination mechanism housed with the CDRRMO OpCen; the two terms are related but are not interchangeable.                                                                                                                 |
| **Post-disaster needs assessment (PDNA)**                              | A structured post-disaster assessment used to estimate the effects and impacts of a disaster and identify recovery and reconstruction needs. The Manual distinguishes it from rapid operational damage and needs assessment.                                                                           |
| **Pre-disaster risk assessment (PDRA)**                                | An assessment undertaken before a hazard impact to inform preparedness, readiness, anticipatory decisions and response planning.                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Quick Response Fund (QRF)**                                          | The portion of the LDRRMF identified in the national DRRM framework for relief and recovery programmes and activities, subject to applicable legal and financial rules.                                                                                                                                |
| **RACI**                                                               | A responsibility-assignment matrix identifying who is Responsible for doing the work, Accountable for the result, Consulted before or during the work, and Informed of the outcome. A RACI allocation clarifies work but does not create legal authority.                                              |
| **Rapid damage assessment and needs analysis (RDANA)**                 | A rapid assessment process used after an event to establish initial damage, effects and priority needs for operational decision-making and response coordination.                                                                                                                                      |
| **Rehabilitation**                                                     | Measures that restore and improve, where appropriate, basic services and facilities, livelihoods and living conditions in affected communities as part of the recovery process.                                                                                                                        |
| **Recovery**                                                           | The restoration and improvement, where appropriate, of livelihoods, health, economic, physical, social, cultural and environmental assets, systems and activities of a disaster-affected community or society, in alignment with sustainable development and the principle of Build Back Better.       |
| **Risk**                                                               | The potential for harmful consequences or losses arising from the interaction of a hazard with exposed people and assets, their vulnerability and their capacities.                                                                                                                                    |
| **Situation report (SitRep)**                                          | A structured operational report that consolidates verified incident information, impacts, response actions, resource status, gaps and priority needs for decision-making and coordination.                                                                                                             |
| **Standard operating procedure (SOP)**                                 | A controlled, step-by-step procedure that specifies its owner, authority, trigger, actors, actions, decision rules, inputs, outputs, records, timing, controls and escalation arrangements.                                                                                                            |
| **State of Calamity**                                                  | A formal declaration made through the authority and process provided by law when the statutory conditions are met. The Manual's procedures guide assessment and recommendation but do not replace the legal declaration process.                                                                       |
| **State of Imminent Disaster**                                         | A formal status under Republic Act No. 12287 and its implementing rules, subject to the applicable legal triggers, authority, procedures and effectivity of national issuances. The Manual treats unresolved national operational parameters as matters for verification.                              |
| **Vulnerability**                                                      | The physical, social, economic and environmental conditions or processes that increase the susceptibility of people, communities, assets or systems to the impacts of hazards.                                                                                                                         |

# How to Use This Manual

This Manual is one document for two bodies: the permanent City DRRM Office (CDRRMO) and the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) that the City activates when needed. Start with the Introduction. It explains the purpose, the legal basis, the assessment and the conventions used in every chapter.

- **To find a procedure**, use the Master Procedure Register (Annex A). It lists every SOP with its chapter, owner, quality stage and key record.

- **To act in an emergency**, go to Chapter 4. Its SOPs run in the order of a real event, from warning receipt to deactivation.

- **To check a legal point**, read the legal framework section (section 4) of the chapter, then the official text. The official text always governs.

- **To see what is still unconfirmed**, read the validation register at the end of each chapter.

Each chapter follows the same pattern: an at-a-glance panel, the assessment findings, purpose and scope, the legal framework, the processes, the SOPs, the RACI, performance measures, the implementation priorities and the references. Tables and figures are numbered by chapter (Table 4.3 is the third table in Chapter 4). Captions follow APA style: number in bold, title in italics, and a note below.

## Quality Management Approach

The Manual applies Total Quality Management (TQM). In practice this means three things. Every process has an owner and a record. Every process is measured. Every gap found becomes a corrective action that is closed only on proof that it worked. The cycle is Plan–Do–Check–Act (Figure FM.1).

|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

Every SOP names who benefits and how they are reached. | Ch4 warning acknowledgement; Ch5 grievance handling; Ch9 inclusive consultation |

| **Element**                    | **What It Records**                                                                            |

# Executive Summary
Ormoc City CDRRMO–EOC Manual of Operations

**Institutionalising Risk-Informed Governance, Operational Readiness, and Deep Resilience**

## 1. Strategic Context and Institutional Transformation

The Ormoc City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO)–Emergency Operations Center (EOC) Manual of Operations (MOO) establishes an integrated institutional and operational framework for strengthening disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) across the City Government of Ormoc and its 85 Philippine Standard Geographic Code (PSGC) barangays.

The Manual addresses a fundamental institutional challenge: translating existing disaster management mandates, operational experience, and inter-agency coordination practices into a coherent, legally anchored, documented, and verifiable system of governance. It connects routine institutional responsibilities with preparedness, anticipatory action, emergency response, recovery, and continuous improvement.

Rather than treating disaster management primarily as an event-driven response function, the Manual positions DRRM as a continuing responsibility of local governance. It establishes institutional arrangements, decision rights, operational procedures, accountability mechanisms, and information systems intended to embed DRRM in planning, budgeting, service delivery, and development processes.

The Manual is assessment-informed and operational by design. Its provisions respond to identified institutional and operational gaps through standard operating procedures (SOPs), responsibility assignments, prescribed records, performance measures, and corrective actions. The MODE (Manual of Operations for the DRRMO and EOC) digital platform is proposed as an enabling environment for controlled documentation, operational monitoring, institutional records, and performance assurance.

### 1.1 Institutional Assessment and Diagnostic Baseline

The Manual draws on the Ormoc CDRRMO–EOC Institutional Assessment Tool (IAT), Version 1.7, dated 11 November 2026. The instrument comprises 140 indicators across 22 domains: Part A covers the CDRRMO (82 indicators in 10 domains); Part B covers the EOC (43 indicators in seven domains); and Part C covers institutional interfaces with other City offices and partners (15 indicators in five domains).

The Institutional Maturity Index (IMI) combines Parts A and B. Part C is reported separately as an Institutional Interface Index and is not added to the IMI.

The baseline indicates that operational experience and existing practices have not consistently translated into approved institutional arrangements, documented controls, demonstrated use, and verifiable evidence of compliance.

### 1.2 Systems Diagnosis and Institutional Leverage Points

Beyond identifying individual compliance gaps, the assessment examines institutional structures and recurring patterns that sustain operational weaknesses. The systems diagnosis highlights three principal archetypes:

- Shifting the burden. Immediate operational demands are repeatedly addressed through temporary staffing, event-specific arrangements, and informal problem-solving. The reported workforce of approximately 47 personnel includes four permanent plantilla employees; this reported figure requires validation against HRMO records.

- Growth and underinvestment. Expanding responsibilities in DRRM, anticipatory action, emergency coordination, and institutional performance have not been matched consistently by investments in permanent staffing, EOC infrastructure, information management, and operational redundancy.

- Drifting goals. Institutional performance risks being measured by emergency response effort rather than demonstrable compliance, preparedness, procedural effectiveness, and sustained improvements in resilience.

The central transformation is from fragmented, event-driven arrangements toward an integrated, continuously functioning, and accountable DRRM operating system.

### 2.1 Integrated Operating Architecture

The architecture links governance and institutional leadership with CDRRMO management, EOC coordination, and incident command. Risk intelligence, operational procedures, and enabling systems are connected through MODE and performance assurance mechanisms.

**Figure ES.2**

*Integrated CDRRMO–EOC Operating Architecture*

![Figure 4: 2.1 Integrated Operating Architecture](/library/moo-consolidated/fig-04.webp)

### 2.2 Principal Institutional Contributions

- **Governance and legal institutionalisation.** Clarifies the responsibilities of the City Mayor, Sangguniang Panlungsod, CDRRMC, CDRRMO, and EOC; identifies the need to formalise EOC authority and distinguish declaration processes.

- **End-to-end operational procedures**. Covers multi-hazard early warning, preparedness, anticipatory action, EOC activation and deactivation, incident coordination, resource mobilisation, reporting, and transition to recovery. Proposed EOC alert postures are White (normal), Blue (partial activation), and Red (full activation), aligned with the National Disaster Response Plan resource postures (White, normal operations; Blue, at least 50% of resources on standby; Red, all resources available).

- **Risk-informed planning and spatial integration.** Connects CDRA findings with CLUP zoning, CDP investment decisions, contingency planning, and Public Service Continuity Planning.

- **Multi-sectoral coordination and accountability.** Establishes responsibility arrangements and institutional interfaces involving barangays, City departments, regional and national agencies, utilities, civil society, academic institutions, and private-sector partners.

- **Digital continuity and quality assurance.** MODE is designed to support controlled records, role-based access, operational logbooks, documented decisions, annual assessments, and corrective action tracking.

## 3. Strategic Priorities and Actionable Institutional Improvements

### 3.1 Governance, Organisational Capacity, and Institutional Authority

The immediate priority is to establish the institutional foundations required for a functioning CDRRMO–EOC system.

- Advance the proposed CDRRMO departmental ordinance amendment through the Sangguniang Panlungsod, consistent with applicable national organisational guidelines.

- Issue an appropriate EOC establishment executive order defining authority, relationship with the CDRRMC and OpCen, activation arrangements, and coordination boundaries with ICS.

- Formalise the three functional divisions: Administration and Training; Research and Planning; and Operations and Warning.

- Develop a permanent staffing and workforce plan, including competency requirements, duty rosters, succession arrangements, and personnel welfare safeguards.

- Designate an Anticipatory Action focal person and formalise institutional responsibilities.

### 3.2 Risk Intelligence, Preparedness, and Operational Readiness

- Establish geospatial information governance and verification procedures for authoritative hazard information from PAGASA, PHIVOLCS, and MGB.

- Mainstream CDRA findings into land-use planning, development investment screening, contingency planning, and public service continuity.

- Develop a City Public Service Continuity Plan supported by Business Impact Analyses and essential-function inventories.

- Establish systematic quality assurance of Barangay DRRM Plans across all 85 barangays.

- Strengthen EOC activation, early warning, reporting, resource coordination, and incident management procedures.

- Conduct exercises to test warning thresholds, operational rosters, inter-office coordination, and the ICS–EOC interface.

### 3.3 Recovery, Rehabilitation, and Build Back Better

- Formulate a Pre-Disaster Recovery Framework identifying sectoral responsibilities, recovery priorities, financing options, and implementation arrangements.

- Designate and develop RDANA and PDNA teams.

- Establish a controlled transition mechanism transferring unresolved response requirements into recovery processes.

- Apply hazard exposure, climate resilience, environmental safeguards, and social inclusion criteria to reconstruction investments.

- Strengthen monitoring and accountability for recovery programmes until completion.

### 3.4 DRRM Financing, Anticipatory Action, and Resource Accountability

The CY 2026 LDRRMF programme approved under CDRRMC Resolution No. 05, s. 2025 amounts to PHP 139,955,741.40. The approved programme comprises a 70% component of PHP 97,969,018.98 and a 30% Quick Response Fund (QRF) of PHP 41,986,722.42.

| **Funding Component**                                                       | **Share / Basis**           | **Amount**        |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|-------------------|
| Prevention, mitigation, preparedness, response, rehabilitation and recovery | 70%                         | PHP 97,969,018.98 |
| Quick Response Fund                                                         | 30%                         | PHP 41,986,722.42 |

- Maintain year-specific Special Trust Fund ageing and utilisation records.

- Establish pre-arranged supplier framework agreements for emergency goods, fuel, and heavy equipment.

- Strengthen procurement, accounting, inventory, and pre-audit controls.

- Maintain verified resource inventories and prepositioned stock plans.

- Improve documentation, tracking, and replenishment of emergency resources.

### 3.5 Monitoring, Evaluation, and Institutional Learning

The Manual establishes a continuous improvement mechanism through the Plan–Do–Check–Act (PDCA) cycle.

- Annual IAT assessment and evidence-based validation.

- Standardised performance monitoring and reporting.

- Structured after-action reviews following incidents, operations, and exercises.

- Centralised Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) tracking.

- Development of a georeferenced Disaster Event and Loss Database.

- Documentation and submission of applicable post-declaration reports within prescribed periods.

### 3.6 Partnerships and Community Resilience

- Formalise technical interface agreements with relevant City Government offices.

- Strengthen coordination with OCD Region VIII, DILG Region VIII, Leyte Province, neighbouring local government units, utilities, and other partners.

- Maintain an updated institutional partner directory and mutual-aid arrangements.

- Institutionalise Barangay Emergency Action Team training and community preparedness programmes.

- Strengthen volunteer accreditation, competency development, deployment arrangements, and insurance coverage.

- Audit designated evacuation centres for structural safety, accessibility, protection, sanitation, and applicable standards.

## 4. Governance Accountability and Responsibility Assignment

The Manual introduces a Master Responsibility Assignment Matrix using the RACI framework to clarify institutional responsibilities and minimise overlapping mandates.

| **RACI Role**   | **Meaning**                                                  | **Application**               |
|-----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Responsible (R) | Performs the work and produces the required output.          | Operational delivery          |
| Accountable (A) | Owns the result and approves the output or decision.         | Decision and result ownership |
| Consulted (C)   | Provides technical, legal, operational, or financial advice. | Two-way technical input       |
| Informed (I)    | Receives relevant information about the decision or outcome. | One-way communication         |

The framework is intended to operate alongside existing legal mandates and approved organisational arrangements. It does not independently transfer statutory authority or replace formal delegations and appointments.

## 5. Implementation Roadmap and Institutionalisation

The Manual proposes a phased implementation approach to sequence legal reforms, operational improvements, and long-term institutional sustainability. The indicative 2027 horizons are proposed targets and remain subject to City Government validation, prioritisation, and approval.

**Figure ES.3**

*Proposed 2027 Institutionalisation Sequence*

*Note.* Indicative horizons proposed in the Executive Summary. Timing, deliverables, accountable offices, and resources require confirmation through City Government decisions.

### Phase 1 – Legal and Structural Foundation (Q1 2027)

Strategic objective: Establish the legal, organisational, and financial foundations of the CDRRMO–EOC operating system.

- Advance the CDRRMO departmental ordinance amendment.

- Issue the EOC establishment executive order and formalise the ICS–EOC coordination boundary.

- Operationalise the State of Imminent Disaster procedure and corresponding reporting arrangements.

- Integrate an anticipatory action funding line into the appropriate LDRRMF investment planning process, subject to legal and budgetary validation.

- Formalise key personnel designations, functional responsibilities, and institutional accountability arrangements.

### Phase 2 – Operationalisation and Pre-Arrangement (Q2 2027)

Strategic objective: Translate approved institutional arrangements into operational capability.

- Execute pre-arranged supplier framework agreements and resource mobilisation protocols.

- Complete quality assurance reviews of Barangay DRRM Plans across all 85 barangays.

- Audit designated evacuation centres and prioritise structural and operational improvements.

- Designate and equip an alternate EOC facility.

- Conduct initial EOC activation, coordination, and relocation exercises.

- Strengthen preparedness inventories, emergency rosters, and partner arrangements.

### Phase 3 – Institutionalisation, Performance Assurance, and Excellence (Q3–Q4 2027)

Strategic objective: Consolidate institutional improvements through continuous monitoring, evidence-based learning, and sustained performance.

- Develop and back-load the historical Disaster Event and Loss Database for 1991–2026.

- Conduct the annual full-scale community simulation exercise involving all 85 barangays, subject to the approved exercise programme.

- Complete annual IAT reassessment and verification of institutional improvements.

- Track and close priority gaps through the central CAPA register.

- Strengthen compliance with applicable Gawad KALASAG and Seal of Good Local Governance disaster management criteria.

The phases provide a proposed sequence rather than an automatic approval or funding commitment. Final implementation schedules, accountable offices, resource requirements, and performance targets must be confirmed through appropriate City Government decisions.

## 6. Expected Institutional Outcomes and Strategic Value

| **Expected Outcome**                                 | **Strategic Value**                                                                                                          |
|------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Stronger and more accountable DRRM governance        | Clearer mandates, decision rights, approval mechanisms, and responsibility assignments.                                      |
| Greater operational readiness and continuity         | Formalised activation, staffing, warning, resource coordination, and continuity arrangements.                                |
| More risk-informed development and investment        | Systematic integration of CDRA into land-use planning, development programming, infrastructure, and continuity planning.     |
| More transparent and accountable resource management | Improved financial controls, anticipatory action arrangements, procurement planning, inventory management, and audit trails. |
| Institutional learning and deep resilience           | Annual assessment, exercises, after-action reviews, CAPA, digital continuity, and leadership succession.                     |

These outcomes should be measured through approved indicators, documented outputs, verified operational performance, and successive IAT assessment cycles rather than through policy issuance or activity completion alone.

## 7. Conclusion and Call to Institutional Action

The Ormoc City CDRRMO–EOC Manual of Operations represents a strategic shift in how the City organises, governs, and sustains disaster risk reduction and management. It moves beyond the conventional view of DRRM as a response-oriented function and establishes an integrated framework connecting institutional governance, risk intelligence, preparedness, anticipatory action, emergency coordination, recovery, financing, partnerships, and continuous improvement.

Its principal contribution is the translation of institutional assessment findings into an actionable operating architecture: defined mandates, assigned responsibilities, documented procedures, required records, performance indicators, and corrective mechanisms.

However, the Manual's effectiveness will depend not on its completion as a document, but on its validation, formal adoption, resourcing, consistent application, and demonstrated use across the City Government and its partner institutions.

The immediate institutional agenda is therefore to:

- Validate the assessment baseline, institutional arrangements, and proposed procedures.

- Secure the appropriate legal and administrative instruments for adoption.

- Assign accountable offices and provide the necessary human, financial, and technical resources.

- Integrate approved procedures into regular City Government operations and the MODE platform.

- Establish annual monitoring, independent verification, and continuous improvement mechanisms.

**The strategic ambition is clear: to institutionalise a safer, more prepared, more accountable, and deeply resilient Ormoc City—where disaster resilience is embedded in governance systems, development decisions, public institutions, and communities.**

## Document Status and Legal Qualification

This Executive Summary reflects the Consolidated Draft 1.0 of the Ormoc City CDRRMO–EOC Manual of Operations dated 12 November 2026. The Manual remains a controlled working draft for technical, institutional, and legal validation. Proposed policies, organisational arrangements, funding mechanisms, and operational procedures do not acquire legal effect solely through their inclusion in the Manual. They require approval or adoption through the appropriate legal and administrative instruments. *The official text governs.*

# Introduction to the Manual

## 1. Purpose and Application of the Manual

This Manual of Operations (MOO) provides one integrated operating reference for the City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (CDRRMO) and the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) of the City Government of Ormoc. It explains how the City's disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) functions are organised and carried out across regular operations, risk assessment, prevention and mitigation, preparedness, early warning, anticipatory action, emergency response, recovery and continuous improvement.

The Manual translates applicable laws, local ordinances, executive and administrative issuances, approved plans, standards and operational guidance into a coherent set of institutional arrangements, procedures, decision pathways, responsibilities and records. It is intended to help personnel understand who is responsible, what action is required, when and under what conditions it is taken, what authority governs the action, what evidence must be recorded, and where an issue must be referred.

The Manual is designed for use by the CDRRMO, the activated EOC, the City offices and service units that contribute to DRRM, barangays, response and recovery partners, and other institutions with defined roles. It is also a reference for orientation, training, exercises, performance review and institutional learning.

Three rules apply throughout the Manual:

- **The Manual does not create legal authority**. It operationalises authority established by law and valid City instruments. Where an additional ordinance, executive order, designation or other instrument is needed, the Manual identifies the requirement for action by the competent authority.

- **A written procedure is not, by itself, proof of institutional capability**. A procedure becomes an established practice when it is appropriately approved, assigned, resourced, used, recorded, reviewed and improved.

- **The Manual and its platform content remain controlled working material until validated and approved through the City's applicable processe**s. Drafting, configuration or platform seeding does not constitute approval.

## 2. Ormoc City and Its Disaster Risk Context

Ormoc City is an independent component city in the Province of Leyte, Eastern Visayas (Region VIII). The City comprises 85 barangays. This is the confirmed current geographic reference for the Manual. Older plans, datasets and historical records may use a previous barangay configuration; where those sources are used, the relevant historical crosswalk must be made explicit so that trends, service coverage and event records are not compared on inconsistent geographic units.

The City's risk context includes multiple interacting natural, biological, technological and climate-related hazards. These include tropical cyclones and associated storm surge; riverine and flash flooding, including areas influenced by the Anilao and Malbasag river systems; rain-induced and earthquake-induced landslides; earthquakes and liquefaction; tsunami; drought and El Niño conditions; epidemics such as dengue; and industrial or geothermal-related incidents. Exposure, vulnerability and service dependencies vary across communities, infrastructure, livelihoods and ecosystems.

Ormoc's disaster experience, including the 1991 flood, Super Typhoon Yolanda in 2013, the magnitude 6.5 Leyte earthquake in 2017 and Typhoon Odette in 2021, reinforces the need for a system that connects risk knowledge to land-use and development decisions, preparedness, warning, coordinated response, recovery and long-term resilience. These events are part of the City's institutional learning context; they do not replace current hazard information or official technical advisories.

The Manual therefore treats risk as a dynamic interaction among hazards, exposure, vulnerability, capacities and dependencies. Hazard information must be drawn from competent and authoritative sources, including PAGASA, PHIVOLCS and MGB, and from City-approved plans and assessments. The Manual does not create independent forecasting products or substitute for official warnings.

## 3. Legal and Policy Basis

The Manual is grounded in the laws, local issuances, guidelines, standards, memorandum circulars, approved plans and other authoritative instruments applicable to the City Government of Ormoc. Its purpose is to harmonise these requirements into a consistent institutional and operational framework so that provisions that are distributed across different instruments can be applied coherently in day-to-day work and during emergencies.

The Manual's principal national legal anchors include Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010; Republic Act No. 10173, or the Data Privacy Act of 2012; and Republic Act No. 12287, or the State of Imminent Disaster and Early Action Act, together with its implementing rules and regulations and applicable subsequent issuances. The relevant local ordinances, executive issuances, administrative guidelines and sectoral rules are identified in the appropriate chapters and controlled legal and policy registers.

The CDRRMO leads the technical and institutional harmonisation of the Manual and coordinates the resolution of operational inconsistencies. This leadership does not displace the statutory or delegated powers of the City Mayor, Sangguniang Panlungsod, CDRRMC, other City offices, national government agencies or other competent authorities. The City Legal Office is engaged where a legal dispute, conflicting legal interpretation or matter requiring formal legal advice arises. OCD Region VIII is consulted or informed, as appropriate to the issue and its mandate.

Where provisions appear inconsistent, the applicable hierarchy of law and valid issuances governs. The Manual must not be interpreted as amending, repealing or overriding an enactment or valid City issuance. References to laws and policies are guides to the governing instruments; the official text governs.

## 4. Structure and Organisation of the Manual

The Manual is organised into ten chapters. The sequence moves from institutional authority and organisational foundations, through risk intelligence and operational action, to recovery, accountability, learning, partnerships, community resilience and long-term sustainability.

**Table I.1**

*Ten-Chapter Architecture of the Manual*

| **Chapter** | **Title**                                                                 | **Primary Focus**                                                                                     |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1           | Legal Mandate, DRRM Governance and Institutional Accountability           | Legal framework, decision rights, governance processes and institutional accountability.              |
| 2           | CDRRMO Organisational Structure, Staffing and Human Resource Management   | Office structure, functional mandates, staffing, competencies, duty systems and workforce continuity. |
| 3           | Risk Intelligence, Planning and Institutional Preparedness                | Risk data, assessments, plans, critical facilities, preparedness and continuity arrangements.         |
| 4           | Early Warning, EOC Activation, Incident Management and Emergency Response | Warning, readiness, activation, coordination, incident management and protective action interfaces.   |
| 5           | Recovery, Rehabilitation and Build Back Better                            | Post-event assessment, recovery governance, rehabilitation, reconstruction and resilience outcomes.   |
| 6           | DRRM Financing, Resource Management and Accountability                    | Financing, budgeting, procurement, logistics, resource tracking and financial accountability.         |
| 7           | Monitoring, Evaluation, Knowledge Management and Continuous Improvement   | Performance monitoring, reporting, learning, corrective action and controlled revision.               |
| 8           | Stakeholder Engagement and Institutional Partnerships                     | Inter-office, intergovernmental, private-sector, civil-society and community partnerships.            |
| 9           | Public Awareness, Community Resilience and Capacity Development           | Risk communication, public awareness, inclusive capacity development and community action.            |
| 10          | Institutional Sustainability, Deep Resilience and Recognition             | Institutional continuity, stewardship, innovation, resilience and recognition pathways.               |

*Note. The chapter sequence is the Manual's content architecture. Functional modules, master requirements, chapters, SOPs, workflows, forms and annexes are related but distinct levels of organisation.*

Each chapter follows a common structure: purpose and scope; chapter-specific findings and requirements; legal and policy references; institutional roles and boundaries; operating arrangements; standard operating procedures (SOPs); responsibility and coordination matrices; performance and quality controls; implementation priorities; forms, registers and annexes; references; and validation or source-control notes. The Introduction explains the common method and conventions so that chapters can focus on their subject matter.

## 5. Assessment Method and Evidence Framework

### 5.1 The Institutional Assessment Tool

The Manual is informed by the Ormoc CDRRMO–EOC Institutional Assessment Tool (IAT), version 1.7. IAT v1.7 is the confirmed controlled assessment instrument for this Manual. It contains 140 indicators organised into 22 domains across three parts: Part A assesses the CDRRMO; Part B assesses the EOC; and Part C examines institutional interfaces with other City offices and partners.

**Table I.2**

*IAT v1.7 Structure*

| **Assessment Part** | **Coverage**            | **Indicators** | **Domains** | **Use**                                                                 |
|---------------------|-------------------------|----------------|-------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| A                   | CDRRMO                  | 82             | 10          | Assesses the office's institutional and functional capacity.            |
| B                   | EOC                     | 43             | 7           | Assesses EOC organisation, readiness and operational capability.        |
| C                   | Institutional interface | 15             | 5           | Assesses coordination and dependencies with other offices and partners. |

*Note. Parts A and B inform the Institutional Maturity Index (IMI). Part C is reported separately as an Interface Index and is not added to the IMI.*

Within Parts A and B, indicators are classified as Mandatory or Good Practice. This distinction supports the assessment of minimum institutional compliance alongside the identification of practices that strengthen performance beyond the minimum. The IAT is an assessment instrument; it does not itself approve an office structure, confer authority or replace the City's legal and administrative decision processes.

### 5.2 Assessment Methods and Evidence

Assessment uses a combination of document review, key informant interviews, focus group discussions and direct observation or site visits, as appropriate to the indicator. Evidence is recorded against the indicator it supports, with its source, date, status and limitations. Informants are identified by office or institutional role in assessment records unless an authorised and lawful purpose requires otherwise. Personal information is handled in accordance with applicable data-protection requirements.

Evidence must distinguish an approved and implemented arrangement from a draft, verbal account, proposal, observed practice or historical record. Where evidence is incomplete, inconsistent or unavailable, the limitation is recorded rather than concealed by an assumed score.

### 5.3 Scoring and Validation

**Table I.3**

*IAT Maturity Scoring Guide*

| **Score** | **Maturity Description** | **Evidence Principle**                                                             |
|-----------|--------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0         | Absent                   | No identifiable arrangement, practice or evidence.                                 |
| 1         | Initial                  | Verbal, informal or ad hoc practice with limited documentation.                    |
| 2         | Developing               | Draft, partial or inconsistently applied arrangement.                              |
| 3         | Compliant                | Approved or formally established arrangement supported by evidence of use.         |
| 4         | Advanced                 | Compliant arrangement with testing, review, learning and demonstrated improvement. |
| NA        | Not applicable           | Use only with a documented justification and validation.                           |

*Note. Maturity bands for index values: Absent below 0.5; Initial 0.5–1.49; Developing 1.5–2.49; Compliant 2.5–3.49; Advanced 3.5 and above. The scoring rubric is applied as defined in controlled IAT v1.7. Interview or FGD statements alone do not establish a score of 3 or 4; supporting documentary or observed evidence is required.*

IAT v1.7 is confirmed as the controlled instrument; the individual scores, evidence records, interpretations and derived results remain subject to validation and verification. The validation process checks whether evidence is relevant, current, attributable and sufficient; whether the scoring rule has been applied consistently; and whether any material disagreement or missing evidence has been resolved or explicitly retained as an open issue.

Assessment results are used to identify maturity gaps, mandatory compliance needs, institutional dependencies and improvement priorities. A score is not a performance judgement about an individual. It describes the documented maturity of an institutional arrangement at the time of assessment.

## 6. Design Principles

The Manual applies five design principles across all chapters and supporting platform functions:

- Compliant. Each requirement is linked to its governing legal, policy or administrative basis. Mandatory obligations are distinguished from recommended or good-practice measures.

- Context-specific. Procedures reflect Ormoc's hazards, confirmed 85-barangay geography, institutional arrangements, service dependencies and local operating conditions.

- Efficient. Procedures are practical and proportionate. Steps, forms and records are designed to support action without unnecessary duplication or administrative burden.

- Evidence-based. Decisions, assessment findings and operational records identify their sources, dates, assumptions, limitations and validation status.

- Actionable. Findings are translated into assigned responsibilities, SOPs, workflows, forms, implementation priorities, performance measures and follow-up actions.

## 7. Systems Thinking, Quality Management and Coherence

Disaster risk is produced and changed through interactions among hazards, exposure, vulnerability, capacities, institutions, infrastructure, ecosystems and social and economic systems. The Manual therefore treats the CDRRMO, EOC, City offices, barangays and external partners as connected parts of one local DRRM system. A gap in one function may affect other functions through information flows, authority relationships, resource dependencies and timing.

Systems thinking is used to examine not only visible events and immediate operational problems, but also recurring patterns, institutional structures, feedback loops and assumptions that influence performance. It helps identify leverage points where clearer mandates, better information, stronger coordination, adequate resources or improved feedback can produce benefits across multiple functions.

Quality management provides the discipline for maintaining and improving this system. Processes should have clear owners, inputs, outputs, decision rules, records and performance measures. The Plan–Do–Check–Act cycle supports implementation, monitoring, review and corrective action. Lessons from exercises, incidents, assessments and audits should inform controlled changes to the Manual and its supporting tools.

Coherence is maintained across five connected layers:

- Legal and policy requirements: the authoritative instruments that establish obligations and decision rights.

- Institutional architecture: the offices, councils, positions and partners that hold mandates and responsibilities.

- Operational processes: the SOPs, workflows, triggers, decision points and escalation routes that translate mandates into action.

- Information and records: the evidence, forms, registers, logs and reports needed to support decisions and accountability.

- Performance and learning: indicators, review, after-action learning and corrective action that strengthen the system over time.

## 8. Institutional Invariants and Authority Boundaries

The following principles apply throughout the Manual. Chapter-specific procedures may provide additional detail but must not contradict these boundaries:

- The CDRRMC is the City's statutory policy, coordination and oversight body under the applicable legal framework. The CDRRMO is the permanent technical and operational office and serves as the CDRRMC secretariat in accordance with its mandate.

- The EOC is an activated coordination mechanism. It is not a fourth CDRRMO division and is not a substitute for incident command. The Incident Commander and Incident Management Team retain field-level incident command; the EOC supports coordination, information management, resource coordination and executive decision support.

- EOC activation, a State of Calamity under Republic Act No. 10121, and a State of Imminent Disaster under Republic Act No. 12287 are distinct processes. One must not be treated as automatically creating or replacing another.

- City offices, national agencies, utilities, barangays and partners retain their own legal mandates. A RACI matrix clarifies responsibility and coordination; it does not transfer statutory authority or create a power that an office does not otherwise hold.

- The Manual does not independently authorise evacuation orders, no-build zones, declarations, expenditure, procurement or other coercive or financial decisions. These actions must follow the authority, process and safeguards established by applicable law and valid City instruments.

- Hazard thresholds and technical triggers must be sourced from competent agencies and approved City plans. The Manual must not invent rainfall, wind, flood, tsunami, earthquake or landslide thresholds.

- Responsibilities are assigned to offices and positions rather than dependent on the continued presence of named individuals. Designations, alternates and succession arrangements must be maintained through appropriate City processes.

- Records must be proportionate and privacy-conscious. Personal information is collected and shared only for a lawful, specified purpose and with appropriate safeguards. A blank or missing report means 'not reported' or 'not available'; it must never be interpreted as zero.

## 9. Review, Validation and Institutional Decision-Making

The Manual is developed through a structured process of technical review, evidence validation, institutional consultation and formal decision-making. These activities are related but distinct. A technical comment may improve clarity or feasibility; evidence validation confirms whether a statement is supported; a recommendation proposes a course of action; and a formal decision is made only by the office or authority empowered to make it.

The CDRRMO leads and coordinates the Manual's technical and institutional review. It identifies the appropriate reviewers and validators, consolidates comments, maintains the issue and decision records, routes matters to the competent office, and tracks resolution. This coordinating role reflects the CDRRMO's ownership of the Manual's operational coherence; it does not replace the decision rights of the Mayor, Sangguniang Panlungsod, CDRRMC or other competent authorities.

OCD Region VIII is consulted or informed where regional technical guidance, coordination or national-to-local alignment is relevant. The City Legal Office is engaged when a legal dispute, conflicting interpretation or need for formal legal advice arises. Subject-matter offices validate matters within their mandates, including organisational and staffing arrangements, planning and risk information, finance and procurement, public information, data protection, response operations and recovery.

The Review and Validation Tracker is a working management instrument. It records review areas, evidence needs, responsible offices, open issues and decisions. Its proposed assignments support coordination and do not, by themselves, constitute formal designations or approvals. The CDRRMO maintains the authoritative status of each issue and ensures that decisions are reflected in the controlled Manual and relevant MODE records.

### 9.1 Validation and Closure Rules

- Every material comment or issue is logged, assigned to an appropriate office or decision owner, and given a clear disposition.

- Evidence is checked against the relevant requirement and its source. Conflicting evidence is recorded and referred for resolution.

- Proposed procedures, role assignments, triggers, thresholds and forms remain marked as proposals until validated and approved through the applicable process.

- A matter is closed only when its disposition, supporting evidence or decision, responsible office and resulting document or platform change are recorded.

- Where a matter remains unresolved, the Manual states the limitation and identifies the required decision or validation action rather than presenting an assumption as settled fact.

## 10. The Manual and the MODE Platform

MODE (Manual of Operations for the DRRMO and EOC) is the digital platform that supports the controlled use, maintenance and operational application of the Manual. The Manual and MODE are related but not interchangeable: the Manual sets out the approved institutional and operational arrangements, while MODE provides digital access to controlled content, workflows, records, evidence and supporting tools.

MODE is intended to help authorised users locate current procedures, complete operational records, coordinate tasks, maintain traceability and support institutional learning. Depending on the user's role and the platform's configured permissions, its functions include access to the Manual and Library, DRRM workflows and protocols, EOC coordination and records, risk and assessment tools, resource and request information, situation reporting, and synchronisation of supported field records.

### 10.1 Controlled Content and Version Management

The Manual, chapters, SOPs, workflows, forms and annexes must be maintained as controlled content. Each item should have a unique identifier, title, version, status, owner, approval reference where applicable, effective date and review history. Draft content must remain visibly distinct from approved content. Platform seeding or publication does not convert a draft into an approved procedure.

### 10.2 Operational Records and Traceability

MODE records should support traceability from a requirement or procedure to the responsible role, action, evidence and resulting decision. Corrections to controlled operational records must preserve the original record and provide an auditable correction history. Reports should show their reporting period, geographic scope, source and status. Missing information must not be represented as a confirmed zero.

### 10.3 Risk Information and External Sources

MODE may organise and present risk information, maps, reference layers and official products for decision support. It does not replace the competent agency that issues warnings, forecasts or technical advisories. Users must check the date, source, geographic coverage and limitations of external information before relying on it.

### 10.4 Offline Use and Synchronisation

Where supported, selected records may be prepared or captured offline and synchronised when connectivity becomes available. Users must follow the platform's sync status and conflict-handling instructions. Offline availability does not mean that every function or decision can be completed without a connection; controlled actions may require authenticated access, current information or an online approval pathway.

### 10.5 Privacy, Security and Access

Access to MODE must be role-based and limited to legitimate operational and institutional purposes. Users must protect credentials, avoid unnecessary collection or disclosure of personal information, and follow the City's data-protection, records-management and information-security requirements. Platform access, system administration and data-protection oversight are separate functions and must not be conflated.

### 10.6 Governance, Custody and Turnover

The CDRRMO is the institutional governance owner of MODE and shall serve as its institutional custodian following formal turnover. Governance includes stewardship of platform content, operational rules, user roles, change control, records, service continuity and alignment with the approved Manual. The CDRRMO shall designate or appoint a separate Data Protection Officer (DPO) through the appropriate City process and consistent with applicable legal and institutional requirements. The DPO's data-protection oversight role must remain distinct from routine platform administration and content custody.

During development and preparation for platform seeding, the Consultant and MODE Systems Architect and Developer temporarily support the reconciliation of chapter, SOP, workflow, form and annex identifiers. This is a time-bound development and configuration responsibility; it does not confer permanent governance or custodianship. The City ICT Office may provide technical support within its mandate, but MODE governance and post-turnover custody remain with the CDRRMO.

Formal turnover should document, as applicable, the approved Manual and source files; platform repository and source-code access; hosting and domain accounts; system architecture and configuration; database and storage arrangements; backup and recovery procedures; security and access controls; data-protection documentation; operating instructions; support arrangements; known limitations; outstanding issues; and the named City personnel responsible for stewardship. The transfer is complete only when the receiving office has verified access, control and the ability to maintain the platform.

### 10.7 Platform Limitations

MODE is a decision-support and operational-management platform. It does not replace statutory decision-makers, official warning agencies, field command, professional judgement, approved plans or required documentary approvals. Users must follow the governing law and City procedures even where a platform workflow provides a convenient sequence or template.

## 11. Behavioural Design and Stakeholder Action: Applying the B = MAP Framework

The Manual and MODE are designed not only to make information available but to help the right people take the right institutional action at the right time. This design uses B. J. Fogg's Behavior Model, expressed as Behaviour = Motivation + Ability + Prompt (B = MAP). The expression is a practical model, not literal arithmetic: the intended behaviour is more likely when motivation, ability and a prompt converge at the same moment.

**Table I.4**

*Applying B = MAP to Manual Review and Institutional Action*

| **Element** | **Meaning in This Project**                                                  | **Design Response**                                                                                              |
|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Behaviour   | The specific action expected from a stakeholder or office.                   | Define observable actions such as review, validate, recommend, decide, provide evidence or close an issue.       |
| Motivation  | The reason the action matters to the institution and the person responsible. | Connect the task to mandate, public safety, institutional responsibility, relevance and accountability.          |
| Ability     | The practical capacity to complete the action.                               | Provide accessible text, clear evidence, manageable tasks, guidance, tools, role clarity and a workable process. |
| Prompt      | A timely cue that calls for a defined action.                                | Issue a specific assignment, notification, instruction, deadline or follow-up with an expected response.         |

*Note. A prompt alone is insufficient when the responsible person lacks the motivation, authority, information, time or practical ability to act.*

A useful prompt should identify who is expected to act; why the action is required; what exact section, evidence or decision is involved; how the action should be completed and against what criteria; when a response is due; what response is expected; and what happens next.

The framework distinguishes stakeholder behaviours from the CDRRMO's coordination behaviours. Stakeholders review, validate, recommend, provide evidence or decide within their mandates. The CDRRMO assigns and clarifies tasks, coordinates review, receives and consolidates inputs, resolves or routes issues, monitors progress and records closure. MODE should be assessed by whether it helps these actions occur with evidence and proper authority—not simply by logins, uploaded documents or feature usage.

## 12. Document Conventions and Instructions for Use

The Manual uses consistent headings, numbering, tables, figures, SOP identifiers, forms, workflows and annex references so that users can find and apply information reliably. The following conventions apply:

- Headings use a consistent hierarchy. Chapter titles are distinct from numbered sections and subsections. The Introduction is front matter and is not an additional chapter.

- Tables are numbered by chapter or front-matter sequence, have a concise Title Case title above the table, and include a note or source statement below where needed. Column headings use Title Case.

- Figures have a sequential number, a concise caption and a source or explanatory note. Conceptual diagrams are identified as explanatory models and are not presented as measured results.

- SOPs use a consistent identifier and control structure. Each procedure should state its purpose, owner, trigger, authority, inputs, steps, decision rules, records, timing, escalation and related forms.

- Forms, workflows, registers and annexes use unique identifiers and cross-references. The same identifier must not be assigned to different items, and an identifier must not be changed in one location without updating all references.

- Responsibilities are expressed by office or position. Personal names may appear in orientation or contact material where appropriate, but operational accountability must not depend on a named individual.

- Status labels distinguish draft, for review, for validation, validated, approved, effective, superseded and archived content. Only the competent authority can approve or adopt a provision.

Before platform seeding, the Consultant and MODE Systems Architect and Developer are responsible for temporarily reconciling the chapter, SOP, workflow, form and annex identifiers across the Manual and its supporting registers. The reconciliation must be recorded and checked before the identifiers are treated as stable platform references.

Users should begin with the chapter relevant to their function, then follow its linked SOPs, forms, registers and annexes. Where a procedure refers to another chapter, the cross-reference should be followed to understand the related authority, resource, information or reporting requirement. Where a conflict or uncertainty is found, users should refer it to the CDRRMO rather than independently rewriting or bypassing a controlled procedure.

## 13. National Issuances, Regulatory Updates and Change Control

Disaster risk reduction, early action, emergency management, financing, procurement, privacy and local governance requirements may be clarified or amended through subsequent laws, implementing rules, administrative issuances and technical guidance. The Manual must therefore be maintained as a controlled and reviewable instrument rather than treated as a static publication.

The CDRRMO should monitor relevant changes through official sources and coordinate an assessment of their implications for the Manual, SOPs, workflows, forms, training and MODE configuration. Where a national rule or technical parameter is not yet issued, is under clarification or requires a local decision, the matter must be recorded with its source, status, responsible office and required action. An anticipated rule must not be presented as already in force.

Changes are incorporated through the Manual's document-control and approval process. A proposed change is assessed for legal consistency, operational impact, resource implications, data-protection implications and effects on related chapters and platform content. The approved version, effective date, change history and superseded material must remain traceable.

## 1. Introduction

This chapter establishes the legal, governance and institutional accountability framework for the City’s CDRRMO and EOC. It defines how the City Government organises, directs, coordinates, monitors and improves its DRRM functions across normal operations, preparedness, anticipatory action, emergency response and recovery, and it sets the decision rights that every later chapter relies on.

This chapter opens directly with its own findings. The purpose of the Manual, the City context, the assessment method (IAT v1.7, evidence rule, maturity bands), the design principles, the systems-thinking and quality approach and the document conventions are set out once in the Introduction to the Manual.

### 1.1 Assessment-Informed Governance Priorities

The October 2026 assessment identifies a significant distinction between the maturity of the CDRRMO, the EOC and their institutional interface.

The assessment also identifies broader system dependencies involving City Planning, Engineering, Budget, Environment, Social Welfare, Health, Education, Utilities and other institutions. These are addressed through the interface arrangements established in this chapter and the succeeding operational modules.

**Management implication**: The priority is not simply to create more committees or issue additional policies. It is to establish a coherent governance system in which each mandate has an accountable owner, each process has a defined workflow, each decision has a legitimate authority, and each institutional output can be verified.

**Assessment interpretation**: The workbook’s Dashboard (IAT v1.7, 11 Nov 2026) reports 1.98/4.00 as the combined Institutional Maturity Index, after the evidence rule (Methodology 5.2) was applied to 15 indicators. Part C is reported separately and is not included in that index. Unscored indicators and provisional desk assessments must not be read as proof of compliance.

### 1.2 Maturity and Compliance in the Governance Domains

The assessment separates institutional maturity from mandatory compliance (Introduction, section 5). A domain can reach a fair maturity index and still be legally non-compliant because one or more Mandatory requirements are below 3. This matters for governance in Ormoc:

- CDRRMO Legal Mandate and DRRM Governance (A1) has a maturity index of 2.47 out of 4.00 but only 66.7% mandatory compliance (4 of 6).

- EOC Legal Basis and Concept of Operations (B1) has a maturity index of 2.23 but only 20% mandatory compliance (1 of 5).

- Across Parts A and B, mandatory compliance is 32.9% against a combined maturity index of 1.98.

Improvements must therefore address both capability and compliance. A practice carried out informally is not yet an institutional control; an executive order, organisational chart or facility does not establish compliance until the requirement is documented, approved, used and evidenced.

### 1.3 What the Consultations and Records Show

The assessment methods are described in the Introduction (section 5.2). The findings below are those that bear on governance.

**Stakeholder position.** All offices consulted (CDRRMO, CPDO, CSWDO and the City Administrator’s Office) share one aim: clear roles and responsibilities for each unit and accountable person, and that these are carried out. All agree that a Manual of Operations will help significantly. This chapter responds by giving each governance function an accountable owner, a workflow and a record.

**Issuance review.** The review of 2021–2024 issuances in October 2026, extended to 1993–2025 in November 2026 (section 4.5), found the following points relevant to governance:

- **Council composition.** The CDRRMC was reorganised by EO No. 2022-0006 and later by EO Nos. 2023-0041 and 2024-032A. The membership register shall carry only the latest EO and its amendments.

- **Warning-driven actions are decided event by event.** Pre-emptive evacuation (CDRRMC Res. No. 09 s.2021) and suspension of work and classes (Res. No. 08 s.2021; Res. No. 06 s.2022) were each adopted by a separate resolution at the time of the event, although Ordinance No. 003, s. 2013 (forced evacuation) and Ordinance No. 135, s. 2023 (suspensions) already set the authority. A pre-set warning–action matrix (A6.2) citing these ordinances shall replace event-by-event resolutions.

- **Declarations.** The SP adopted a State of Calamity for Typhoon Odette (SP Res. No. 2021-366). The CDRRMC recommended a one-year State of Calamity for the 2024 dengue outbreak (Res. No. 06 s.2024). See Process 4 (GOV-04).

- **Odette response decisions.** The Council approved a PHP 2 M standby fund for prepositioning food and non-food items (Res. No. 11 s.2021) and asked LEYECO V to run its 2 MW standby generator during widespread outages (Res. No. 10 s.2021). It also sent cash aid from the 2021 Quick Response Fund to other LGUs (SP Res. Nos. 2021-365, -367 and -369). No standing mutual-aid agreement exists (A10.1).

- **Planning and funding.** The Council approved the DRRM 10-Year Plan (Res. No. 01 s.2023), and EO No. 2022-00020 created the DRRM Plan Technical Working Group. The flood control and drainage master plan was funded in 2023 (Res. Nos. 03, 04 and 07 s.2023; about PHP 11.0 M), but no output was sighted.

- **Records control.** The files of CDRRMC Res. Nos. 03 and 04 s.2022 contain each other’s text; the CCCM Executive Order is filed as No. 263 but the scan reads 243; SP Res. No. 2021-357 still cites 110 barangays. These findings support GOV-02 and GOV-08.
