**Requesting augmentation.** When City capacity is or will be exceeded, the EOC prepares a request that states the need, quantity, location, time needed and the City's own resources already committed. The Mayor, as CDRRMC Chair, sends it to the Province, and through the Province to the region where national assets are needed, as the National Disaster Response Plan and the regional SOPs provide (SOP 8-03). The RA 12287 request for a State of Imminent Disaster is the one exception that goes directly from the CDRRMC to the RDRRMC VIII, under Chapter 1, SOP GOV-05. Incoming national or provincial teams are received at a staging area, briefed and tasked through the EOC, and work under the Incident Commander.

## 8. Horizontal Coordination: Mutual Aid With Other LGUs

Ormoc's neighbours (Kananga, Albuera, Merida and Isabel) share its watersheds, roads and hazards. A flash flood in the Anilao and Malbasag catchment, an earthquake on the Philippine Fault or a geothermal incident can affect several of them at once, or overwhelm Ormoc while its neighbours are spared. RA 7160 Sec. 33 allows LGUs to coordinate efforts, services and resources by agreements approved by their sanggunians. The IAT recommends **technical mutual aid agreements**, framed between DRRM offices for defined resources, so that cooperation does not depend on political alignment.

**Table 8.7**

*Elements of a Technical Mutual Aid Agreement*

| **Element**                 | **Content**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Parties and authority       | The LGUs, each acting through its Mayor with prior sanggunian authority; the Province may join.                                                                                                                                                         |
| Scope                       | Defined resource types: search and rescue teams, emergency medical teams, heavy equipment, water tankers, communications, evacuation centre capacity, technical staff (engineers, damage assessors, CCCM staff); information sharing on shared hazards. |
| Activation                  | By written or recorded request from the requesting LGU's Mayor or authorised DRRM officer; the assisting LGU may decline if its own area is threatened.                                                                                                 |
| Command and safety          | Resources work under the host LGU's Incident Commander under ICS, keep their own supervisors, and may be withdrawn by the sending LGU for its own emergency.                                                                                            |
| Duration and demobilisation | Default period per deployment, renewable; demobilisation through the host EOC with a handover record.                                                                                                                                                   |
| Costs                       | Who bears travel, fuel, food and lodging; how any reimbursement is settled; consumables replaced in kind or paid.                                                                                                                                       |
| Liability and insurance     | Each LGU insures its own personnel and equipment; treatment of injury, damage and third-party claims.                                                                                                                                                   |
| Information                 | Shared contact directory, warning and SitRep exchange; data protection under Chapter 7.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Exercise and review         | At least one joint exercise or call-down test a year; annual review; term and renewal.                                                                                                                                                                  |

*Note. Annex 8-B gives a model outline. Terms are to be negotiated by the parties and reviewed by the City Legal Office; this chapter fixes none of them.*

Watersheds that extend beyond the City (C3.2) are a natural first subject: the Anilao–Malbasag and Pagsangaan catchments link upstream land use to downstream flood risk, and an agreement on information sharing and joint monitoring with DENR, EDC and the upstream LGUs can be negotiated alongside mutual aid. The 10-Year Plan's planned Leyte DRRMCs Telecom and Response Network is the route for joining a provincial network.

## 9. Private Sector and Utilities

Private firms and utilities own much of what keeps the City running: power generation and distribution, transmission, telecommunications, water, fuel, transport and supplies. Some are also hazard sources (the geothermal field, industrial sites) and all are themselves exposed.

**Table 8.8**

*Private-Sector and Utility Partners*

| **Partner**                                         | **Before an Event**                                                                                               | **During and After an Event**                                                                      |
|-----------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| EDC Leyte Geothermal (CDRRMC member)                | Shared hazard information; joint exercises for geothermal incidents; Project TRANSFORM and NRC programmes         | Emergency notification for incidents on its sites; equipment and personnel support under agreement |
| LEYECO V (CDRRMC member) and NGCP                   | Restoration-priority list (hospitals, EOC, evacuation centres, water pumps); standby generation; contact protocol | Outage reports to the EOC; restoration in agreed priority (SOP 8-05)                               |
| Telecommunications providers                        | Cell-on-wheels and backup power arrangements; emergency alert broadcasts under RA 10639                           | Network status reports; priority restoration                                                       |
| Water service (City Waterworks and other providers) | Rationing and tanker plans                                                                                        | Water supply status; tanker deployment                                                             |
| Chamber of Commerce and businesses                  | Business continuity outreach on shared hazard scenarios (C5.1); a seat for the private sector on the CDRRMC       | Information on business disruption; voluntary support through the donations process (Chapter 6)    |
| Suppliers under framework agreements                | Agreements under Chapter 6 (SOP 6-06)                                                                             | Call-offs and deliveries                                                                           |

Engagement with the private sector is transparent. No partner receives preference in procurement because of a partnership; purchases follow Chapter 6 and RA 12009. Members of the CDRRMC declare any interest in a matter before the Council.

## 10. Civil Society, Volunteers, Faith-Based and Humanitarian Organisations

- **CSOs on the CDRRMC.** The five CSO seats are filled by organisations accredited by the SP; their representatives bring community knowledge and reach. SOP 8-06 sets how seats are filled and renewed.

- **Volunteer groups.** Organised groups such as the CPR-RIMT Rapid Rescue Riders work under signed MOAs that state training, equipment, tasking, insurance and liability. Individual community disaster volunteers are accredited under RA 10121 Sec. 13 (Res. No. 07, s. 2024) and the City volunteer programme (Ordinance No. 160, s. 2024); Chapter 9 trains them. Spontaneous volunteers in an event are registered and tasked through the EOC, never deployed unregistered.

- **Philippine Red Cross.** As an auxiliary to the government in the humanitarian field (RA 10072), the Red Cross sits on the CDRRMC and the CCCM Team; its roles in first aid, welfare, blood services and restoring family links are agreed in advance.

- **Faith-based groups.** Churches, mosques and other faith communities often shelter evacuees and distribute relief. No agreement with any faith-based group was found. The CDRRMO invites them to the annual partner forum and agrees, where they wish, on the use of their facilities as evacuation sites (subject to the Building Official's safety check) and on relief coordination.

- **CCCM partners.** The City CCCM Team (EO of 2022) brings partners into camp management under the JMC No. 02, s. 2021 standards; their roles are part of the partner register.

- **Sectoral groups.** Organisations of persons with disabilities, older persons, women, children and youth are invited to planning, exercises and reviews, so that plans reflect their needs (with the PDAO, OSCA and GAD focal point).

## 11. Academe, Science and Development Partners

The City's academic and scientific partners give it research, data, training and technical review it could not afford alone: the tertiary institutions under the Education Resilience and DRRM Coordination Group (CDRRMC Res. No. 04, s. 2025), the City College of Ormoc and EVSU Ormoc, the Oscar M. Lopez Center (SP Res. No. 2021-357), the National Resilience Council and EDC through Project TRANSFORM. Their work is recorded in the partner register with its outputs. Research that uses City data follows a data-sharing agreement (Chapter 7, SOP 7-09). Development partners and donors are engaged through the same register; funds and goods they provide follow Chapter 6.

## 12. Communities and Accountability to Affected People

Barangays are the City's closest partners. Their BDRRMCs plan, warn, evacuate and report; Chapter 9 builds their capacity and Chapter 4 coordinates them in events. This chapter adds two commitments. First, communities have a way to raise concerns and suggestions about DRRM services at any time, through the CDRRMO hotline and feedback desk, and partners working in communities use the same channel. Second, the City reports back: the annual results report (Chapter 7) is published, and the CDRRMO explains to barangays what changed after major events.

## 13. The Partner Register and the Partnership Lifecycle

Every DRRM relationship with a written basis is recorded in the partner register (PTN-F01) and follows the lifecycle in Figure 8.4. An agreement is counted as a commitment only when it is authorised, signed, in force and filed. The register is reviewed at a CDRRMC meeting each year before the typhoon season.

## 15. Responsibility Assignment (RACI)

| **\[R\] Responsible** | **\[A\] Accountable** | **\[C\] Consulted** | **\[I\] Informed** |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|---------------------|--------------------|

"A" is the single proposed process-accountable owner; "R" performs; "C" is consulted; "I" is informed. The RACI allocates work; it does not transfer legal powers.

**Table 8.26**

*RACI for Stakeholder Engagement and Partnerships*

| **Activity**                            | **MY** | **SP** | **CC** | **HD** | **AT** | **RP** | **EOC** | **LG** | **LO** | **PT** | **CA** |
|-----------------------------------------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|---------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Partner register and agreements         | A      | A      | C      | R      | R      | I      | I       | R      | C      | R      | I      |
| Inter-LGU mutual aid agreement          | A      | A      | C      | R      | R      | C      | C       | R      | –      | R      | I      |
| Mutual aid activation                   | A      | I      | I      | R      | C      | –      | R       | –      | –      | R      | I      |
| Augmentation request and incoming teams | A      | I      | I      | R      | C      | C      | R       | –      | C      | R      | I      |
| Part C interface agreements and review  | I      | –      | I      | R      | C      | R      | –       | C      | A      | –      | A      |
| Utility restoration arrangements        | A      | A      | I      | R      | C      | C      | R       | C      | C      | R      | I      |
| CDRRMC partner seats                    | A      | A      | C      | R      | R      | –      | –       | R      | –      | C      | I      |
| Annual partner forum                    | I      | I      | A      | R      | R      | C      | C       | –      | C      | C      | I      |
| Assistance to other LGUs                | A      | A      | C      | R      | R      | –      | –       | C      | C      | –      | I      |

*Note. MY = City Mayor; SP = Sangguniang Panlungsod; CC = CDRRMC; HD = CDRRMO Head; AT = CDRRMO Administration and Training; RP = CDRRMO Research and Planning; EOC = EOC Manager and staff; LG = City Legal Office; LO = Part C lead offices; PT = partner organisation or LGU; CA = City Administrator. Where a row has two "A" entries, each holds a distinct act: the SP authorises and the Mayor signs; for Part C, each lead office is accountable for its own indicators and the City Administrator approves interface agreements; for the CDRRMC seats, the SP accredits CSOs and the Mayor issues the EO.*

## 20. Concluding Notes

Ormoc already has more partners than many cities: national agencies, utilities, a geothermal operator and five CSOs on its Council; a resilience partnership with the NRC and EDC; volunteers under agreement; tertiary institutions in a coordination group; and a record of helping its neighbours. What is missing is the standing arrangement that makes each relationship dependable on the worst night: a signed mutual aid agreement, a restoration-priority list, an interface agreement with each City office that owns part of the risk, and a register that shows which commitments are real.

Writing these procedures does not create the partnerships. Until the partner register holds signed agreements, at least one mutual aid agreement is in force and has been exercised, the Part C lead offices have signed interface agreements, and the first partner forum has been held, this chapter remains a controlled working draft.

## Annex 8-B. Model Outline of a Technical Mutual Aid Agreement

**Table 8.32**

*Outline of a Technical Mutual Aid Agreement*

| **No.** | **Article**                     | **Content to Be Negotiated**                                                                                   |
|---------|---------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1       | Parties and authority           | LGUs; sanggunian resolutions authorising each Mayor; optional accession by the Province                        |
| 2       | Purpose and principles          | Technical cooperation in DRRM; reciprocity; no transfer of authority; each party first protects its own people |
| 3       | Definitions                     | Requesting party, assisting party, resources, deployment, host Incident Commander                              |
| 4       | Resources covered               | Types of teams, equipment and services; annexed lists updated yearly                                           |
| 5       | Activation                      | Who may request; request content; response time; right to decline                                              |
| 6       | Command, control and safety     | Under the host IC (ICS); own supervisors; right of recall                                                      |
| 7       | Logistics                       | Self-sufficiency period; food, lodging and fuel arrangements                                                   |
| 8       | Costs and settlement            | What each party bears; reimbursement method; timing                                                            |
| 9       | Liability and insurance         | Personnel and equipment insurance; claims; indemnity                                                           |
| 10      | Information and data            | Directory, warnings and SitRep exchange; data protection                                                       |
| 11      | Exercises and review            | Annual joint exercise or call-down; annual review                                                              |
| 12      | Term, amendment and termination | Duration; renewal; notice period                                                                               |

# Public Awareness, Community Resilience and Capacity Development

## 1. Introduction and Assessment-Informed Rationale

A warning works only if people understand it and know what to do. A contingency plan works only if the people named in it have practised it. A barangay can account for its residents within hours only if its BDRRMC is organised, trained and has done it before. This chapter is about those people: the public, barangay officials and volunteers, school and hospital staff, City office personnel and the EOC roster. It sets how the City builds their awareness and their skills, and how it keeps those skills from fading.

Chapter 2 develops the CDRRMO's own staff (competency framework, training needs analysis and SOP HR-04). Chapter 4 issues warnings and notices during events. This chapter covers capacity beyond the CDRRMO and between events: public awareness, the City's annual DRRM training and exercise programme, barangay and community resilience, volunteers, and the readiness of schools, hospitals and evacuation centres.

The baseline shows activity without measurement (Figure 9.1). Domain A7 (Preparedness and Community Capacity) has an index of **2.12 (Developing)**, with 2 of 5 Mandatory items compliant. Training, drills and IEC happen, but most scores rest on the FGD alone and fell to 2 under the evidence rule: the training calendar, drill evaluations, IEC reach and BDRRMC functionality are all still to be shown. Evacuation centres do not yet meet the Ligtas Pinoy Centers standards (A7.4, High). There is no refresher cycle (A7.8), no skills inventory across offices and barangays (A2.10), and no record of a barangay accounting for its residents within a set time (A7.9) (Table 9.1).

### 1.1 What the Records Show

- **Training mandates and plans.** CDRRMC Res. No. 09, s. 2024 adopts the Incident Command System and directs the CDRRMO to train City and barangay officials and responders in it. The CDP 2024–2030 programmes standard training modules (PPA 1.1.6), capacity building for CDRRMC agencies and BDRRMCs, a local pool of trainers and simulation exercises (PPAs 2.6.1 to 2.6.3), school DRRM coordinator training (PPA 2.16) and the ACDV roster, insurance and training (PPAs 2.7.1 to 2.7.3). The 10-Year Plan lists ICS at all levels, EOC management, MDM, CCCM, RDANA and PDNA training. No training needs analysis covering offices and barangays was found.

- **Community health and volunteers.** Ordinance No. 171, s. 2024 institutionalises Barangay Health Emergency Response Teams in all barangays. Ordinance No. 160, s. 2024 institutionalises the City volunteer programme under RA 9418. CDRRMC Res. No. 07, s. 2024 approves the accreditation of community disaster volunteers; Res. Nos. 03 and 04, s. 2022 cover their guidelines and insurance. The CPR-RIMT Rapid Rescue Riders augment HEMS and the CDRRMO under SP Res. No. 2023-347.

- **Barangay plans.** EO 2023-0085 created the Barangay DRRM Plan Review Team, led by the CDRRMO Head with the CPDO, using the Enhanced Quality Assurance System of NDRRMC MC No. 03, s. 2022 (Chapter 3). Certificates of review were not in the document set.

- **Evacuation centres.** The 10-Year Plan plans retrofits of 30 evacuation centres, mostly open covered courts, and MOAs for private alternate centres. The CDRA rates evacuation centres and covered courts "Poor" for vulnerability. The IAT recommends auditing centres against RA 12076 and DSWD standards and prioritising the 46 critical flood barangays.

- **Inclusion.** The IPGDO sits on the CDRRMC. CDP PPAs 1.2.6 (gender-sensitive and inclusive EWS SOP), 2.1 (inclusive IEC and risk communication) and 2.20 (Comprehensive Emergency Program for Children) are planned.

- **Schools.** CDRRMC Res. No. 04, s. 2025 creates an Education Resilience and DRRM Coordination Group with all tertiary institutions; DepEd SDO, the Red Cross and DOH-CHD HEMS sit on the CDRRMC; Ordinance Nos. 135, s. 2023 and 189, s. 2025 set rules on suspending classes and work.

### 1.2 Design Considerations

1.  **Competence, not attendance.** A training counts when the person can do the task, shown in an exercise or real event. Attendance sheets are records, not proof.

2.  **Capacity drains.** Staff move, barangay officials change after each election, and unused skills fade. Every capacity has a refresher date (Figure 9.2).

3.  **Practise in order.** Drills, then tabletop exercises, then functional and full-scale exercises; each evaluated, each finding tracked.

4.  **Barangay first.** The first responders in Ormoc are its 85 BDRRMCs and their puroks. Support goes first to the barangays that are least functional and most exposed.

5.  **Reach, not activity.** IEC is measured by the people and households reached and what they know or do, not by the number of seminars held.

6.  **Inclusive by design.** Messages, trainings, drills and evacuation centres are designed with women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities and other at-risk groups, not adjusted afterwards.

## 2. Purpose and Intended Results

This chapter sets how the City builds and sustains awareness and capacity for disaster risk reduction and management across its people, communities and institutions.

Intended results:

1.  An annual City DRRM training programme, based on a needs analysis of City offices, BDRRMCs, schools, responders and volunteers, is approved and delivered, with evidence of competence (A7.1).

2.  Every trained role has a refresher date, and attendance and lapse are tracked (A7.8); a skills inventory across offices and barangays is updated every 12 months (A2.10).

3.  An annual exercise programme, from NSED drills to an EOC functional exercise and a full-scale exercise, is run and evaluated (A7.2, B7.3).

4.  An IEC programme with annual reach targets per barangay is delivered in Cebuano and accessible formats (A6.4, A6.6), under an approved risk communication plan (A6.5).

5.  All 85 BDRRMCs are assessed for functionality each year, low-functioning barangays receive a support package (A7.3), and each barangay can account for residents of affected puroks within 12 hours (A7.9).

6.  The volunteer programme has a registry, accreditation, insurance, training and deployment rules (A2.8).

7.  Evacuation centres are audited against national standards and improved in priority order (A7.4); schools and hospitals take part in planning and drills (A7.7).

8.  Sector representatives confirm that they were engaged in plans, trainings and drills (A7.6).

## 5. Systems Thinking: Capacity as a Stock

Capacity behaves like water in a tank with a leak (Figure 9.2). Training fills it; staff turnover, barangay elections and unused skills drain it. A City that trains intensively once and then stops will see its capacity fall back within a few years, however good the training was. Two levers matter more than the size of any single course: a refresher cycle and regular exercises, which slow the drain, and a skills inventory, which shows how full the tank is.

**Figure 9.2**

*Capacity as a Stock With Inflows and Outflows*

![Figure 97: Capacity as a Stock With Inflows and Outflows](/library/moo-consolidated/fig-97.webp)

*Note. Prepared for this chapter after Meadows (2008). Each barangay election is a planned outflow that the training calendar should anticipate.*

- **Plan for the outflow.** After each barangay election, the CDRRMO runs an orientation for new BDRRMC members early in their term.

- **Trainers multiply capacity.** A local pool of trainers (CDP PPA 2.6.2), drawn from the CDRRMO, BHERTs, volunteers and partners, lets the City reach 85 barangays without waiting for outside courses.

- **Exercises are where capacity is proven.** Each evaluated exercise is evidence for the IAT at levels 3 and 4.

## 6. Public Awareness and Risk Communication

### 6.1 The IEC Programme

The IEC programme sets, for each year, the messages, audiences, channels and reach targets per barangay (A6.6). Messages follow the hazards and plans of Chapter 3: what each warning means, where the evacuation centre is, what to bring, how to check on neighbours, and what a State of Imminent Disaster is and what anticipatory actions it may bring. Reach is counted as people or households reached, by barangay, sex and age group where possible, and a short knowledge check is used in a sample of barangays each year.

**Table 9.4**

*IEC Channels and Their Use*

| **Channel**                                             | **Use**                                                   | **Reach Measure**                                        |
|---------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| Barangay assemblies and purok meetings                  | Hazard maps, evacuation routes, family plans              | Attendance by barangay and purok                         |
| Schools (with DepEd SDO and tertiary institutions)      | Learner and family preparedness; drills                   | Learners and schools reached                             |
| Local radio and social media                            | Seasonal reminders; explainers on warnings                | Listenership or reach reported by the outlet or platform |
| Printed and visual materials                            | Posters at evacuation centres, health centres and markets | Places posted and checked                                |
| Community events (fiestas, market days)                 | Booths and demonstrations                                 | Visitors counted                                         |
| Sector organisations (PWD, older persons, women, youth) | Messages designed with and for them                       | Members reached; feedback received                       |

### 6.2 Local Language and Accessible Formats

Messages are written in Cebuano as spoken in Ormoc, with English where needed, and tested with residents before use (A6.4). Each core message has accessible versions: Filipino Sign Language video (RA 11106), large-print and pictorial versions, plain-language audio, and visual alerts for Deaf and hard-of-hearing residents. Where a message relays an official PAGASA or PHIVOLCS product, the translation keeps its meaning and the original wording is kept on file (Chapter 4).

### 6.3 Risk Communication Plan and Public Information Officer

The City designates a DRRM public information officer and an alternate, and adopts a risk communication plan (A6.5) that sets spokespersons, approval of messages, coordination with the City Information Office, media relations, monitoring of rumours and misinformation, and correction. Between events the plan governs the IEC programme; during events Chapter 4 governs what is issued and by whom.

### 6.4 Preparing the Public for Anticipatory Action

RA 12287 adds a new message: the City may declare a State of Imminent Disaster and ask people to act days before impact. The IEC programme explains this before any declaration, so that the public notices issued under Chapter 4 (A6.7) are understood when they come. Geographically isolated barangays are reached through their BDRRMCs and VHF radio, not only by mobile networks.

## 7. The City DRRM Training Programme

### 7.1 Needs Analysis and Annual Plan

Each year the CDRRMO, with the HRMO, analyses training needs across City offices, the EOC roster, BDRRMCs and BHERTs, schools, responders and volunteers, using the competency matrix (Annex 9-B), the skills inventory, IAT gaps and AAR findings (SOP 9-01). The analysis for CDRRMO staff is done under Chapter 2 (HR-04) and folded in. The result is one annual City DRRM training plan with courses, target groups, providers (CDRRMO trainers, OCD VIII, DOH, DSWD, BFP, Red Cross, academic partners), schedule, cost and evaluation method, funded through the LDRRMFIP (Chapter 6).

### 7.2 Delivery, Records and Evidence of Competence

Training records state the course, provider, dates, participant (by position and office, or barangay), competency addressed, assessment result and refresher date (CAP-F03). Records of City employees are also sent to the HRMO. Competence is shown by assessment at the end of the course and by performance in an exercise or event. MODE does not yet hold training records; until it does, CAP-F03 is kept as a controlled register.

### 7.3 Refresher Cycle

*Note. Intervals are proposals of this chapter for CDRRMC adoption, except where a certifying body sets its own. Attendance and lapse are tracked on CAP-F03 (A7.8).*

### 7.4 Skills Inventory

Every 12 months the CDRRMO updates an inventory of DRRM-relevant skills across the CDRRMO, CDRRMC member offices, BDRRMCs, BHERTs and accredited volunteers: search and rescue, first aid, engineering, logistics, GIS, damage assessment, PDNA, MHPSS, communications, and languages including Filipino Sign Language (A2.10). It records the number of people with each skill by office or barangay and the date of their last training. It feeds the needs analysis and the EOC's surge planning (Chapter 2).

## 8. Drills and Exercises

The City exercises its plans in a progression (Figure 9.3). Drills test one task (evacuation of a school, a siren test, a call-down). Tabletop exercises test plans and decisions around a scenario. Functional exercises activate the EOC against a simulated event without deploying field teams. Full-scale exercises bring the EOC, field teams and partners together. Each is planned with objectives, evaluated under Chapter 7 (SOP 7-04) and followed by tracked actions.

## 9. Barangay and Community Resilience

### 9.1 BDRRMC Functionality and Support

Every year the CDRRMO, with the DILG City Office, assesses the functionality of all 85 BDRRMCs (A7.3), using the DILG barangay preparedness assessment (Listo si KAP, as cited in IAT v1.7) and the City's functionality matrix (CAP-F06): organisation, plan reviewed (Chapter 3), early warning, evacuation, BHERT, equipment, drills held and reporting. Barangays are grouped into three support tiers (Figure 9.4). Low-functioning barangays and those with the highest exposure in the CDRA receive a priority package; higher-functioning barangays become peer mentors.

**Figure 9.4**

*Tiered Support for Barangay DRRM Committees*

![Figure 99: Tiered Support for Barangay DRRM Committees](/library/moo-consolidated/fig-99.webp)

*Note. Prepared for this chapter. Tier thresholds are set by the CDRRMC from the first assessment; none is fixed here.*

### 9.2 Accounting for Residents Within 12 Hours

After an event, each affected barangay should be able to say, within 12 hours of impact, how many of its residents are safe, injured, missing or displaced, purok by purok (A7.9). The BDRRMC does this through purok leaders using the household lists the barangay already keeps, and reports counts, never names, to the EOC. The welfare check is practised in the hazard-specific drill and timed (CAP-F07). Named lists stay with the barangay and the CSWDO (Chapter 7, SOP 7-09).

### 9.3 Barangay Health Emergency Response Teams

Ordinance No. 171, s. 2024 provides for BHERTs in all barangays. Their training and refreshers are part of the City training plan, with the City Health Office, and their readiness is part of the BDRRMC functionality assessment.

## 10. Volunteers

The City volunteer programme (Ordinance No. 160, s. 2024) and the accreditation of community disaster volunteers (Res. No. 07, s. 2024) give the City a reserve of trained people. Chapter 2 (section 14.3) sets the HR rules: volunteers supplement and never replace required positions, and their roles, supervision, safety, insurance and limits are documented. This chapter runs the programme (SOP 9-07): recruitment, accreditation, registry, training, insurance under the risk categorisation adopted in 2022, and deployment rules. During activation, volunteers are tasked through the EOC or the Incident Commander, not directly by the organisations that recruited them. Accredited volunteers may be given anticipatory action tasks under RA 12287 IRR Rule IV Sec. 5, such as helping with pre-emptive evacuation and checking on at-risk households. Spontaneous volunteers in an event are registered at a single point and tasked, or politely redirected.

## 11. Evacuation Centres, Schools, Hospitals and Inclusion

### 11.1 Evacuation Centre Standards

Evacuation centres are audited against RA 12076, DSWD standards and the NDRRMC Disaster Preparedness Minimum Standards (SOP 9-08; Annex 9-D): location in a low-risk area; structural safety (the Building Official's assessment under Chapter 8, C2.1); WASH facilities separated by sex; privacy and family spaces; ground-floor priority and access for persons with disabilities, older persons and pregnant women; child-friendly spaces; a health and first-aid area; security; kitchen and storage; and power and communications. Retrofits are prioritised for centres serving the 46 critical flood barangays and those rated "Poor" in the CDRA, and funded through the LDRRMFIP (Chapter 6). Schools are used as evacuation centres only as a last resort and for the shortest time, consistent with RA 10821.

### 11.2 Schools and Hospitals

DepEd SDO schools, the tertiary institutions in the Education Resilience and DRRM Coordination Group, and the City's hospitals and health facilities take part in contingency plan tabletop exercises and in drills each year (A7.7). Their own preparedness plans remain theirs; the CDRRMO aligns triggers (class suspension under Ordinance Nos. 135, s. 2023 and 189, s. 2025; hospital surge) and communications with them. Education and health anticipatory actions are Part C items owned by DepEd and the CHO (Chapter 8).

### 11.3 Inclusive DRRM

Women, children, older persons, persons with disabilities, indigenous peoples and other at-risk groups take part in designing messages, trainings, drills and evacuation centre improvements, through the IPGDO, the PDAO, the OSCA and their organisations. Once a year, a short consultation with sector representatives asks whether they were engaged and what should change, and their answers are recorded as evidence for A7.6 (CAP-F05). Data on participation and reach are disaggregated by sex, age and disability where this can be done without identifying anyone.

## 12. MODE Support

MODE holds the EOC roster and designations (Chapter 2), the protocols run in drills (each run is a record), barangay reports and resource requests, and the Library and Vault where training materials and exercise reports are kept. It does not yet hold training records, the skills inventory, the BDRRMC functionality matrix or the volunteer registry. Until it does, these are kept on CAP forms as controlled registers; section 16 lists the platform additions. Any future table holding volunteer or trainee personal data follows Chapter 7 (SOP 7-09): positions and counts in reports, names only where the City as employer or programme owner needs them, with access limited by role.

## 13. Standard Operating Procedures

Each SOP has a control block and a step table. Every step states the actor (a position or office, never a person), the action and decision rule, inputs and outputs, and timing, control and escalation. Form codes are those of section 17. All MODE templates named here are proposals; none of SOPs 9-01 to 9-09 is yet loaded in MODE.

## 14. Responsibility Assignment (RACI)

| **\[R\] Responsible** | **\[A\] Accountable** | **\[C\] Consulted** | **\[I\] Informed** |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|---------------------|--------------------|

"A" is the single proposed process-accountable owner; "R" performs; "C" is consulted; "I" is informed. The RACI allocates work; it does not transfer legal powers.

**Table 9.25**

*RACI for Awareness, Community Resilience and Capacity Development*

| **Activity**                            | **MY** | **CC** | **HD** | **AT** | **RP** | **EOC** | **HR** | **SW** | **DI** | **BR** | **SC** |
|-----------------------------------------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|---------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| TNA, skills inventory and training plan | I      | C      | A      | R      | C      | C       | R      | C      | C      | R      | C      |
| Training delivery and refreshers        | –      | I      | A      | R      | C      | C       | R      | C      | I      | R      | C      |
| Annual exercise programme               | I      | A      | R      | R      | C      | R       | –      | C      | C      | R      | C      |
| IEC programme                           | I      | I      | A      | R      | C      | –       | –      | C      | C      | R      | R      |
| Risk communication plan and PIO         | A      | I      | R      | C      | –      | C       | –      | –      | –      | –      | C      |
| BDRRMC functionality and support        | I      | C      | A      | R      | R      | –       | –      | C      | R      | R      | C      |
| Volunteer programme                     | I      | A      | R      | R      | –      | R       | C      | C      | –      | C      | –      |
| Evacuation centre audit and improvement | I      | A      | R      | C      | R      | –       | –      | R      | –      | R      | C      |
| Sector consultation on inclusion        | I      | I      | A      | R      | C      | –       | –      | C      | –      | C      | R      |

*Note. MY = City Mayor; CC = CDRRMC; HD = CDRRMO Head; AT = CDRRMO Administration and Training; RP = CDRRMO Research and Planning; EOC = EOC Manager and staff; HR = City HRMO; SW = CSWDO; DI = DILG City Office; BR = barangays and BDRRMCs; SC = sector organisations (through the IPGDO, PDAO and OSCA). For the volunteer programme, the CDRRMC accredits; for evacuation centres, the CDRRMC sets priorities and the Building Official decides structural safety.*

| 3       | Risk Intelligence, Planning and Institutional Preparedness                | Supplies hazards, scenarios and contingency plans for messages and exercises; reviews barangay plans.                                       |
| 4       | Early Warning, EOC Activation, Incident Management and Emergency Response | Issues warnings and notices that the IEC programme prepares people for; runs evacuation; tasks volunteers.                                  |
| 5       | Recovery, Rehabilitation and Build Back Better                            | Uses trained PDNA and recovery teams; recovery communication follows the risk communication plan.                                           |
| 6       | DRRM Financing, Resource Management and Accountability                    | Funds training, exercises and EC retrofits; uses rotated stocks in drills.                                                                  |
| 7       | Monitoring, Evaluation, Knowledge Management and Continuous Improvement   | Evaluates exercises; holds the CAPA register; reports reach and functionality in the annual results report.                                 |
| 8       | Stakeholder Engagement and Institutional Partnerships                     | Brings partners, schools, hospitals and neighbouring LGUs into trainings and exercises.                                                     |
| 10      | Institutional Sustainability, Deep Resilience and Recognition             | Uses training, exercise and community records as evidence for Gawad KALASAG and SGLG, and plans for capacity that outlasts terms of office. |

## 19. Concluding Notes

The City already trains, drills and informs, and it has put BHERTs, volunteers and school partnerships into ordinance and resolution. What it lacks is the evidence that these activities produce capacity, and the rhythm that keeps capacity from draining away: a needs analysis, a refresher date for every skill, a progression of exercises, a functionality check for every barangay, a reach target for every message, and evacuation centres that meet the standard.

Writing these procedures does not build capacity. Until the first combined training plan has been delivered with competence records, the first EOC functional exercise has been evaluated, all 85 BDRRMCs have been assessed and the evacuation centre audit has begun, this chapter remains a controlled working draft.

# Institutional Sustainability, Deep Resilience and Recognition

## 1. Introduction and Assessment-Informed Rationale

Chapters 1 to 9 set what the City does to reduce, prepare for, respond to and recover from disasters, how it pays for it, how it learns, whom it works with and how it builds capacity. This chapter asks a different question: how do these gains last? A good Manual can be shelved by the next administration; a trained team can leave; a platform can lapse when an account is not renewed; an award can be won one year and lost the next. Sustainability is the work of making the system outlast the people who built it.

The chapter has three parts. **Institutional sustainability** (sections 5 to 7) keeps the legal, human, financial and digital foundations in place. **Recognition** (section 8) treats Gawad KALASAG and the SGLG as independent evidence of progress, not as goals in themselves. **Deep resilience** (section 9) sets the path beyond compliance: fewer losses, faster recovery and adaptation to a changing climate, measured against the Sendai Framework and the Ten Essentials that the City's own plan adopted.

The baseline shows where sustainability is weakest (Figure 10.1). Three of the gaps that carry the most weight in the whole assessment are about permanence: the legal basis of the CDRRMO as a regular office with its JMC 2014-1 divisions (A1.1, High), the filling of the minimum plantilla (A2.3, High) and the alternate EOC (B2.7, score 0, High). Continuity of public services (A3.4) and digital continuity and security (B3.3, B3.5) are still developing. The CDRRMO Head is permanent (A2.2), the EOC has its own budget line (B7.5), and the City takes part in recognition systems (A10.7), but the succession order, the readiness self-check (B7.6) and the follow-up of recognition gaps are not yet documented (Table 10.1).

### 1.1 What the Records Show

- **A legal basis exists, but not the full structure.** Ordinance No. 008, s. 2014 (26 June 2014), amended by Ordinance No. 011, s. 2015, creates the CDRRMO under the Office of the City Mayor with a Head (SG-23) and three LDRRMO I posts. Chapter 1 recasts the A1.1 finding as an amendment of that ordinance to provide the three JMC 2014-1 divisions and their staffing (Annex 1-A), and proposes an EO establishing the EOC (Annex 1-C).

- **People.** The CDRRMO Head holds a permanent position. The FGD reported about 47 staff, of whom four are permanent; most are on job-order or casual terms. The CDP 2024–2030 programmes the creation of regular positions (PPAs 1.1.1–1.1.2) and the 10-Year Plan lists 4 + 4 + 2 plantilla items. SP Res. No. 2023-347 records the CDRRMO's lack of response manpower.

- **Recognition goals.** The CDP sets the goal of achieving the Gawad KALASAG award every year and full compliance with the SGLG disaster preparedness indicators. The 10-Year Plan cites the Gawad KALASAG Seal and the SGLG and observes that the City's performance has been assessed mainly through such national systems.

- **Networks for deeper resilience.** The City has an MCR2030 commitment, the NRC Resilient LGU partnership (SP Res. No. 2021-036) and the EDC Adopt-a-City programme, and is the model LGU of the DENR–EDC Project TRANSFORM (EO 2023-0026). The 10-Year Plan bases its monitoring on the UNDRR Ten Essentials.

- **The platform.** MODE runs in a Supabase project under an organisation named for the City Government of Ormoc, in Tokyo (ap-northeast-1), and on a Vercel team, both on free tiers during development (ADR-026). The architecture decisions require City ownership, time-boxed developer access removed at turnover, portability to any Postgres host, and a decision by the City on paid, City-owned hosting with backups before MODE is used for real operations. Weekly backup and quarterly restore runbooks exist in the repository.

### 1.2 Design Considerations

1.  **Institutions, not individuals.** Every critical role has an alternate and a succession order; every critical document has an owner office and a version; every agreement names positions.

2.  **Law before budget, budget before people.** An office that exists in ordinance and has a line in the budget survives changes of leadership better than one that exists by practice.

3.  **Continuity is tested, not assumed.** The alternate EOC, the PSCP, the backups and the offline mode are proven once a year.

4.  **Recognition is evidence.** Awards confirm progress measured independently; chasing scores for their own sake drifts toward paperwork.

5.  **The City owns its system.** Data, code, accounts and keys belong to the City and can be run by a local IT contractor without the developer.

6.  **Beyond compliance.** Compliance is the floor. The aim is fewer deaths, smaller losses and faster recovery, measured over years.

## 2. Purpose and Intended Results

This chapter sets how the City keeps its DRRM institutions, people, funds, systems and knowledge in place over time; how it uses recognition systems; and how it plans its progress from compliance toward deeper resilience.

Intended results:

1.  The CDRRMO has a full legal basis with its JMC 2014-1 divisions, and the EOC is established by issuance (A1.1, B1.1).

2.  Every critical position has an alternate and a documented succession order, and leadership transitions follow a handover protocol (A2.2).

3.  The PSCP, the alternate EOC and the EOC readiness self-check are tested every year (A3.4, B2.7, B7.6).

4.  MODE runs on City-owned, paid hosting with backups, restore tests, an access review and an information-security policy before it is used for real operations (B3.3, B3.5; MR-10).

5.  The City takes part in the Gawad KALASAG Seal and the SGLG each year, and every gap found is entered in the CAPA register and acted on (A10.7).

6.  A sustainability review each year checks that the legal, human, financial, digital and knowledge foundations are still in place, and updates the resilience roadmap.

7.  At the end of the engagement, the Manual and MODE are handed over to City custody with no dependence on the developer.

## 3. Scope, Application and Institutional Boundaries

**In scope:** the annual sustainability review; legal permanence of the CDRRMO and EOC; leadership succession and transition; financial sustainability lines; continuity testing (PSCP, alternate EOC, readiness self-check); digital continuity and information security of MODE and EOC systems; recognition systems; the resilience roadmap and innovation pipeline; stewardship and handover of the Manual and MODE.

## 5. Institutional Sustainability

Five foundations keep the City's DRRM system standing (Figure 10.2). If any one is missing, the others carry more weight than they can bear: a well-funded office without legal permanence can be dissolved; a well-written Manual without trained people is not used; a platform without backups can lose years of records in a day.

**Figure 10.2**

*Foundations of Sustainable DRRM in Ormoc*

![Figure 101: Foundations of Sustainable DRRM in Ormoc](/library/moo-consolidated/fig-101.webp)

*Note. Prepared for this chapter. The foundation (approved Manual, IAT cycle and CAPA register) is set in Chapters 1 and 7; the five pillars are checked each year in the sustainability review (SOP 10-01).*

### 5.1 Legal and Institutional Permanence

The CDRRMO already exists in ordinance. Permanence now means amending Ordinance No. 008, s. 2014 so that it provides the JMC 2014-1 divisions (Administration and Training, Research and Planning, Operations and Warning) and their functions and staffing; establishing the EOC by issuance with its levels, activation authority and roster; keeping the CDRRMC constituted with all its seats; and keeping the Manual approved and versioned. The sustainability review tracks each instrument (SUS-F01): drafted, endorsed, enacted, implemented.

### 5.2 People and Succession

The Head, the division chiefs, the EOC Manager and the duty officers each have a named alternate and a written order of succession (Chapter 2, section 11.2). When a holder leaves, is on leave or is unavailable in an emergency, the alternate acts without waiting. After each local election, or when the CDRRMO Head changes, a transition protocol (SOP 10-02) briefs the incoming Mayor and CDRRMC on the City's risks, the Manual, open CAPA items, the budget lines and any declaration in force, and confirms the designations that the new administration must reissue. Critical knowledge held by one person is written into the Manual, a protocol or the Vault.

### 5.3 Financial Sustainability

Recurring costs that keep the system working are budgeted as lines, not found event by event: EOC operations and maintenance (B7.5), equipment preventive maintenance and replacement (A8.3, B7.6), stock replenishment (Chapter 6), training and exercises (Chapter 9), insurance (A4.7), and the hosting and support of MODE once the City adopts it for real operations. The sustainability review checks that each line is in the LDRRMFIP and in use (Chapter 6, FIN-F03).

## 6. Continuity of Operations

The City must keep its essential DRRM functions running when the EOC building, its power, its network or its people are affected by the same disaster. The PSCP (Chapter 3) names the essential functions and how they continue; the alternate EOC (Chapter 2, section 2.8) gives a second site; the EOC readiness self-check (B7.6) confirms both are ready. This chapter sets one annual continuity check (SOP 10-04) that brings the three together: a relocation drill to the alternate EOC, a PSCP exercise for the CDRRMO's essential functions, and the EOC Capability Assessment Checklist for both sites. Findings go to the CAPA register.

## 7. Digital Continuity and Information Security

MODE now holds the Manual, the assessment, the protocols, the logbook, the Vault and the EOC's operating records. Its continuity is part of the City's continuity. The architecture already favours it: the data are plain Postgres and SQL migrations that can move to any Postgres host; the app works offline for routine tasks and keeps authority actions online-only; the City owns the project; the developer's access is time-boxed. What remains is to put the operating controls in place and test them (Figure 10.3).

## 8. Recognition Systems

### 8.1 Gawad KALASAG Seal for LDRRMC’s, CY 2026

The Gawad KALASAG Seal for Local DRRM Councils and Offices is governed by NDRRMC MC No. 03, s. 2025 (11 April 2025), and its CY 2026 conduct by OCD Memo No. 763, s. 2026. All 1,724 provinces, cities and municipalities are assessed. The LGU self-assesses with the prescribed LDRRMCO Assessment Tool, attaches its means of verification and a notarised Omnibus Sworn Statement, and submits to OCD Region VIII, whose Regional Validation Committee runs a desk review and may validate in the field. Results for CY 2026 are due not later than 30 November 2026. Special Awards are suspended for CY 2026 pending a supplemental guideline.

An LGU that fails any of six minimum requirements is acknowledged for participation but cannot be recognised. Table 10.5 sets them against the City's records. This is the CDRRMO's own reading for planning; only OCD Region VIII rates the City.

**Table 10.5**

*Gawad KALASAG CY 2026 Minimum Requirements and the City's Records*

| **No.** | **Minimum Requirement (OCD Memo No. 763, S. 2026)**                                                                               | **City Record (for Validation)**                                                                                | **Related IAT and Chapter** |
|---------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| a       | Established and organised LDRRMC                                                                                                  | EO 2024-032A reorganises the CDRRMC; it meets at least quarterly.                                               | A1.2, A1.3; Chapter 1       |
| b       | Membership of non-state stakeholders in the LDRRMC (4 CSOs and 1 private sector)                                                  | Five CSO and two private-sector seats in EO 2024-032A; SP accreditation of the CSOs not shown.                  | A1.2; Chapter 8 (SOP 8-06)  |
| c       | Established LDRRM Office                                                                                                          | Ordinance No. 008, s. 2014 as amended by No. 011, s. 2015.                                                      | A1.1; Chapter 1             |
| d       | Permanent and functional LDRRM Officer compliant with JMC 2014-1                                                                  | Permanent Head appointed; qualification records and JMC 2014-1 staffing to be confirmed.                        | A2.2, A2.3; Chapter 2       |
| e       | Established and functional Operations Center                                                                                      | 24-hour OpCen duty observed in October 2026; roster and handover records to be attached.                        | B4.3; Chapters 2 and 4      |
| f       | Approved and adopted LDRRMP, reviewed by the reviewing authority, covering the assessment year and consistent with the NDRRM Plan | DRRM 10-Year Plan 2023–2032 adopted by SP Res. No. 2023-112; review by the reviewing authority to be confirmed. | A3.1; Chapter 3             |

*Note. Requirements quoted from OCD Memo No. 763, s. 2026, p. 4. The "City record" column is a planning reading for validation, not a rating.*

Above the minimum, the LGU is scored on six criteria with 39 indicators in all (Figure 10.4). The weighted average sets the recognition: Gold at 2.50 and above, Silver at 2.00 to 2.49, Bronze at 1.50 to 1.99.

**Figure 10.4**

*Gawad KALASAG CY 2026 Criteria, Number of Indicators and Weights*

![Figure 103: Gawad KALASAG CY 2026 Criteria, Number of Indicators and Weights](/library/moo-consolidated/fig-103.webp)

*Note. From OCD Memo No. 763, s. 2026, section 5.1 (applying NDRRMC MC No. 03, s. 2025) and section 6 (recognition tiers).*

### 8.2 Seal of Good Local Governance

The SGLG under RA 11292 includes disaster preparedness among its assessment areas. Its criteria are set each year by the DILG and change from year to year, so this Manual does not fix them. Each year the CDRRMO obtains the current criteria from the DILG City Office, maps them to the IAT and the Manual, and prepares the evidence through the Vault (SOP 10-05).

### 8.3 Using Recognition as Evidence

The IAT and the recognition systems measure overlapping things in different ways. Annex 10-B maps the Gawad KALASAG criteria to IAT domains so that one body of evidence in the Vault serves both. Results and assessor comments are entered in the CAPA register like any other finding. The City does not create documents only to satisfy an assessor; every document filed as evidence must also be in use. The MODE Gawad KALASAG self-check tool is to be updated to the CY 2026 tiers before it is used (Coherence Analysis, open issue II.2-2).

## 9. Deep Resilience: Beyond Compliance

Compliance with the IAT Mandatory items and the Gawad KALASAG minimum requirements is the floor. Deep resilience is measured by outcomes: fewer deaths and missing persons, fewer people affected, smaller economic losses, less disruption of basic services, and faster recovery (Sendai Targets A to D), and by the City's position on the UNDRR Ten Essentials, which the 10-Year Plan adopted as the base of its monitoring.

### 9.1 The Resilience Roadmap

**Figure 10.5 proposes three horizons aligned with the LDRRMP 2023–2032 and the Sendai Framework. The first institutionalises what the Manual sets out; the second consolidates it through practice and the plan's mid-term evaluation; the third deepens it toward Sendai 2030 and the next LDRRMP. Within each horizon the order of work follows this priority order: legal constitution first, then the operating systems that carry whole domains, then high-leverage compliance items. Targets for the IMI, Mandatory compliance and the Interface Index are set by the CDRRMC; this chapter sets none.**

**Figure 10.5**

*Proposed Resilience Roadmap, 2026–2032*

![Figure 104: 9.1 The Resilience Roadmap](/library/moo-consolidated/fig-104.webp)

*Note. Prepared for this chapter. Horizons and their contents are proposals for CDRRMC decision; they follow the LDRRMP period (2023–2032), its mid-term report (2029) and the Sendai Framework (2015–2030).*

### 9.2 Deepening Areas

- **Anticipatory action maturity.** From the first funded AA line and the first declaration under RA 12287 toward impact-based triggers, pre-agreed actions by sector and evaluated results (Chapters 4, 6 and 7).

- **Climate adaptation and nature-based solutions.** Linking the LDRRMP with the LCCAP 2019–2030 and Project TRANSFORM: watershed protection in the Anilao–Malbasag catchment, mangrove restoration and climate-smart agriculture (Chapter 8, Part C).

- **Risk-informed development.** Bringing CDRA scenarios into the CLUP and CDP and screening investments (Part C, C1), so that new risk is not created.

- **Social protection and inclusion.** Connecting relief and recovery with social protection and livelihood programmes so that the poorest recover first (Chapter 5).

- **Learning city.** Peer learning through MCR2030 and the NRC, and contributing Ormoc's own lessons to other LGUs (Chapter 7).

### 9.3 Innovation Pipeline

New ideas (a sensor network, a community feedback tool, a new financing instrument) are tried as pilots with a stated purpose, a measure of success, a time limit and a data-protection check; evaluated; and then adopted into the Manual, scaled or dropped (SOP 10-06). A pilot is not a programme until it has been evaluated. Adopted innovations are shared with peers through Chapter 7.

## 10. Stewardship and Handover of the Manual and MODE

The Manual and MODE were developed with the City under a fourteen-week engagement. Their value lasts only if the City can keep, revise and run them alone. At the end of the engagement, and again whenever a custodian changes, the stewardship protocol (SOP 10-07) confirms that the City holds the approved Manual and its source files, the Library versions, the repository, the hosting accounts and keys, the runbooks, the training materials and the handover record; that the developer's access has been removed; and that a named City custodian and a local IT contractor can maintain the platform. The Manual is revised under Chapter 7 (SOP 7-08) and approved only by the CDRRMO Head.

## 11. Standard Operating Procedures

Each SOP has a control block and a step table. Every step states the actor (a position or office, never a person), the action and decision rule, inputs and outputs, and timing, control and escalation. Form codes are those of section 15. All MODE templates named here are proposals; none of SOPs 10-01 to 10-07 is yet loaded in MODE.

## 12. Responsibility Assignment (RACI)

| **\[R\] Responsible** | **\[A\] Accountable** | **\[C\] Consulted** | **\[I\] Informed** |
|-----------------------|-----------------------|---------------------|--------------------|

"A" is the single proposed process-accountable owner; "R" performs; "C" is consulted; "I" is informed. The RACI allocates work; it does not transfer legal powers.

**Table 10.20**

*RACI for Sustainability, Recognition and Deep Resilience*

| **Activity**                             | **MY** | **SP** | **CC** | **HD** | **RP** | **AT** | **CA** | **HR** | **ICT** | **DPO** | **LG** |
|------------------------------------------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|---------|---------|--------|
| Annual sustainability review and roadmap | I      | I      | A      | R      | R      | C      | C      | C      | C       | –       | –      |
| Legal permanence instruments             | A      | A      | C      | R      | R      | C      | C      | C      | –       | –       | R      |
| Leadership transition and succession     | A      | I      | I      | R      | C      | R      | R      | R      | C       | –       | C      |
| Digital continuity and security          | A      | –      | I      | C      | –      | C      | C      | –      | R       | R       | C      |
| Annual continuity check                  | I      | –      | I      | A      | C      | R      | C      | C      | R       | –       | –      |
| Gawad KALASAG and SGLG                   | A      | I      | C      | R      | R      | C      | I      | –      | –       | –       | –      |
| Innovation pipeline                      | I      | –      | C      | A      | R      | C      | –      | –      | C       | C       | –      |
| Stewardship and handover                 | A      | –      | I      | R      | C      | C      | C      | –      | R       | C       | C      |

*Note. MY = City Mayor; SP = Sangguniang Panlungsod; CC = CDRRMC; HD = CDRRMO Head; RP = CDRRMO Research and Planning; AT = CDRRMO Administration and Training; CA = City Administrator; HR = City HRMO; ICT = City ICT office; DPO = City Data Protection Officer; LG = City Legal Office. For legal permanence the SP enacts ordinances and the Mayor issues executive orders.*

## 17. Concluding Notes for Chapter 10 and the Manual

Ormoc has learned at great cost what disasters do: the 1991 flash flood, Yolanda, the 2017 earthquake and the typhoons since. It has built a Council, an Office, a fund, plans, partnerships and a record of helping others. This Manual gathers those pieces into one system and adds the controls that let the City see whether the system works and fix it when it does not.

The test of the Manual is not its approval but its use: a warning turned into action in time, an anticipatory action funded before impact, a family that finds a safe evacuation centre, a barangay that counts its people within hours, a recovery that builds back safer, a lesson that changes a procedure. This last chapter asks the City to protect that system from the slow forces that erode institutions, and to keep raising its standard year after year.

Writing these procedures does not make the system last. Until the CDRRMO's full legal basis is enacted, the alternate EOC has been drilled, MODE runs on City-owned hosting with a tested restore, the first sustainability review has been held and the stewardship handover is complete, this chapter remains a controlled working draft.
